entries.meaning: To put up with something; in older usage, to stay or dwell somewhere.
examples: I cannot abide people who talk during a movie.
She could not abide the noise from the construction site.
He has never abided criticism well.
We abided by the ruling even though we disagreed.
Everyone here abides by the same rules.
The company has abided by every term of the settlement.
Her family abode in that valley for four generations.
The shepherds have abode in these hills since before the road was built.
A strange quiet abides in that house.

senses.head: Tolerate, put up with
body: Almost always negative — cannot abide, could not abide. This is the only sense alive in everyday American English, and it takes the regular abided. (терпеть, выносить)
examples: I cannot abide people who talk during a movie.
She could not abide the noise from the construction site.
He has never abided criticism well.

senses.head: Abide by — comply with
body: Fixed phrasal use, and always regular: abided by, never the strong form. (соблюдать, следовать (правилам))
examples: We abided by the ruling even though we disagreed.
Everyone here abides by the same rules.
The company has abided by every term of the settlement.

senses.head: Dwell, remain
body: Archaic and literary. This is the sense that takes abode, which survives far more healthily as a noun — a humble abode. (обитать, пребывать)
examples: Her family abode in that valley for four generations.
The shepherds have abode in these hills since before the road was built.
A strange quiet abides in that house.

entries.register: formal — legal and literary; abide by belongs to rules and rulings, and the dwelling sense is older still
entries.third person: abides · -ing form: abiding (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: In everyday American English the past is the regular abided, and it is the only choice in abide by: We abided by the ruling. Abode belongs to older and literary writing, and it survives most healthily as a noun — a humble abode.
entries.verb type: stative in the living cannot abide sense — an attitude, not an act, so the progressive is odd: ✗ I am abiding the noise. Action — dynamic only in the archaic dwelling sense (her family abode in that valley).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the tolerate sense, where the object is obligatory (I cannot abide people who talk; ✗ I cannot abide); intransitive in the dwelling sense (a strange quiet abides in that house) and in the prepositional abide by the ruling.
entries.passive: restricted — the stative tolerate sense resists it: ✗ the noise could not be abided by her. The prepositional passive works in legal writing: every term of the settlement was abided by. The dwelling sense is intransitive and has none.
entries.phrasal verbs: abide by

entries.meaning: To come down and settle on something, or to step down out of a vehicle.
examples: Sparrows alight on the feeder the moment I go back inside.
A cardinal alit on the railing and stared at us.
The same dragonfly has alit on that reed all afternoon.
She alights at the Franklin Street stop every morning.
Two passengers had alit before the conductor noticed the open door.
Her eye alighted on the one sentence that mattered.
We have alit on a compromise that might actually work.

senses.head: Land, settle on something
body: The core sense, used of birds, insects, and anything that comes lightly to rest. Both alit and the regular alighted are standard. (садиться, опускаться (о птице, насекомом))
examples: Sparrows alight on the feeder the moment I go back inside.
A cardinal alit on the railing and stared at us.
The same dragonfly has alit on that reed all afternoon.

senses.head: Step down from a vehicle
body: Formal, and commonest in transit announcements and British signage; ordinary American speech says get off. (сходить, высаживаться (из транспорта))
examples: She alights at the Franklin Street stop every morning.
Two passengers had alit before the conductor noticed the open door.

senses.head: Alight on — happen upon
body: Literary, used of a gaze or a thought coming to rest on something. Usually regular here: alighted on. (натолкнуться (на мысль, решение))
examples: Her eye alighted on the one sentence that mattered.
We have alit on a compromise that might actually work.

entries.register: rare — recognized but seldom produced; Americans say land or get off
entries.contrast: Both alit and the regular alighted are standard; Americans write alighted a little more often. Keep the verb apart from the adjective alight, meaning on fire — the barn was alight — which has no past tense at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a verb of motion and coming to rest (a cardinal alit on the railing). Keep it apart from the adjective alight, meaning on fire, which is not a verb form at all.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in every sense — what is landed on or stepped out of comes after a preposition (alight on the feeder, alights at the Franklin Street stop, alighted on a compromise), never as a bare object: ✗ she alit the railing.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so there is no object to promote: ✗ the railing was alit. The barn was alight is the adjective, not a passive.

entries.meaning: To look after someone else's children while the parents are out.
examples: I baby-sit for the Novaks most Friday nights.
She baby-sat my nephews all through high school.
We have baby-sat for them twice this month already.
My brother baby-sits whenever he needs gas money.
Somebody has to baby-sit the build until it finishes.
He baby-sat the server all night waiting for the migration to clear.
I have baby-sat that spreadsheet for three days.

senses.head: Look after children
body: The everyday sense. Modern American style writes the word solid — babysit, babysat — and the hyphen now looks dated. (сидеть с детьми, работать няней)
examples: I baby-sit for the Novaks most Friday nights.
She baby-sat my nephews all through high school.
We have baby-sat for them twice this month already.
My brother baby-sits whenever he needs gas money.

senses.head: Keep an idle watch over something
body: Informal and slightly resentful: to sit with a process or a person that ought not need supervising. (нянчиться с чем-л., присматривать (перен.))
examples: Somebody has to baby-sit the build until it finishes.
He baby-sat the server all night waiting for the migration to clear.
I have baby-sat that spreadsheet for three days.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary American; only the hyphen is dated
entries.contrast: It follows sit exactly. Modern American style writes the word solid — babysit, babysat, babysitting — and the hyphen now looks dated.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a work verb, and equally at home in the informal sense of watching a process that should not need watching (baby-sit the build).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the child or the process as object (she baby-sat my nephews, he baby-sat the server all night), intransitive when the object is left out (I baby-sit for the Novaks most Friday nights).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive uses — the twins were baby-sat by a neighbor, that migration got baby-sat all night. No passive of the bare intransitive she baby-sits on Fridays.

entries.meaning: To light something from behind.
examples: We backlight the product shots to lift them off the wall.
The photographer backlit her subject with a single strobe.
They have backlit every sign in the terminal.
He backlights the stage with two amber panels.
The keyboard had been backlit in blue since the last update.
Every display in the lobby is backlit around the clock.

senses.head: Light from behind
body: Photography and stage lighting. Like light, it also allows a regular backlighted, but backlit is far commoner. (подсвечивать сзади)
examples: We backlight the product shots to lift them off the wall.
The photographer backlit her subject with a single strobe.
They have backlit every sign in the terminal.
He backlights the stage with two amber panels.

senses.head: Backlit — lit from behind
body: Almost always passive or in front of a noun: a backlit screen, a backlit keyboard. (с подсветкой (об экране, клавиатуре))
examples: The keyboard had been backlit in blue since the last update.
Every display in the lobby is backlit around the clock.

entries.register: rare — a photography and display term; the participle backlit does most of the work
entries.contrast: It follows light, including the option of a regular backlighted. Backlit is far commoner, especially in front of a noun: a backlit screen.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a causative lighting verb. The participle backlit has gone on to work as a plain adjective: a backlit screen, a backlit keyboard.
entries.transitivity: transitive only, and the object is obligatory — the photographer backlit her subject; ✗ the photographer backlit is incomplete.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the commoner form — every display in the lobby is backlit around the clock, the keyboard had been backlit in blue.

entries.meaning: To slip back into a bad habit, an abandoned belief, or an earlier and worse condition.
examples: Dieters backslide around the holidays.
He backslid the week after he quit smoking.
She has backslid twice since January.
The preacher warned that a believer can backslide without ever noticing it.
Two of the congregation had backslid by the following spring.
The department backslides every time the budget tightens.
Several districts have backslid on reading scores.
By March the government had backslid on every reform it promised.

senses.head: Relapse into an old habit
body: The everyday sense, used of diets, sobriety, and any effort at self-improvement. (срываться, скатываться назад)
examples: Dieters backslide around the holidays.
He backslid the week after he quit smoking.
She has backslid twice since January.

senses.head: Fall away from faith
body: Religious register, and the original sense. In that writing you will also meet the participle backslidden. (отступаться от веры)
examples: The preacher warned that a believer can backslide without ever noticing it.
Two of the congregation had backslid by the following spring.

senses.head: Regress, lose ground
body: Of institutions, countries, or measured results. Common in journalism: democratic backsliding. (регрессировать, откатываться назад)
examples: The department backslides every time the budget tightens.
Several districts have backslid on reading scores.
By March the government had backslid on every reform it promised.

entries.register: neutral — ordinary in writing about diets, faith, and democracy; less common in speech
entries.third person: backslides · -ing form: backsliding (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: It follows slide. You will also meet the participle backslidden in religious writing, but backslid is the ordinary American form.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a process verb of gradual relapse, used of dieters, believers, and institutions alike (democratic backsliding).
entries.transitivity: intransitive in all three senses — what is lost ground on takes a preposition (backslid on reading scores, backslid on every reform), never a direct object: ✗ she backslid her diet.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so nothing can be promoted to subject: ✗ the reform was backslid. Only the noun backsliding carries the sense in passive-shaped writing.

entries.meaning: To father a child; more broadly, to cause something to come into being.
examples: Violence begets violence.
Cheap money can beget speculation.
That one decision has begot a decade of lawsuits.
The scandal had begot three investigations before anyone resigned.
Abraham begot Isaac.
He had begotten seven children by the time he was forty.

senses.head: Give rise to, cause
body: The living use, and it lives mostly in aphorisms and headlines. Formal; ordinary speech says leads to. (порождать, вызывать)
examples: Violence begets violence.
Cheap money can beget speculation.
That one decision has begot a decade of lawsuits.
The scandal had begot three investigations before anyone resigned.

senses.head: Father a child
body: Biblical and formal, and only ever of the father. The archaic participle begotten is the form most Americans recognize — his only begotten son. (порождать, зачинать (о мужчине))
examples: Abraham begot Isaac.
He had begotten seven children by the time he was forty.

entries.register: formal — biblical and aphoristic; ordinary speech says father or lead to
entries.contrast: It follows get. The archaic participle begotten is the form most Americans actually recognize, from scripture — his only begotten son — while begot is the plainer modern participle. The verb itself is formal or biblical; ordinary speech says father or lead to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a causative verb, formal and aphoristic (violence begets violence) or biblical (Abraham begot Isaac).
entries.transitivity: transitive, with an obligatory object in both senses — cheap money can beget speculation; ✗ violence begets alone says nothing.
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical but stilted in the causal sense (a decade of lawsuits was begot by that decision); the passive that Americans actually meet is the frozen archaic participle his only begotten son.

entries.meaning: To look at something, especially something striking.
examples: The crowd beheld the eclipse in complete silence.
Few travelers have beheld that valley under snow.
She beholds the city each morning from the same window.
Behold the size of that canyon.
He opened the box and — behold — the missing part was inside.
We drove all that way and, lo and behold, the museum was closed.
I looked again and, lo and behold, the keys were sitting on the counter.
Nobody who had beheld the wreck could describe it calmly.

senses.head: Look upon, gaze at
body: Literary or ceremonial; nobody says it in ordinary conversation. Do not confuse it with the adjective beholden, meaning indebted, which is a different word. (созерцать, взирать)
examples: The crowd beheld the eclipse in complete silence.
Few travelers have beheld that valley under snow.
She beholds the city each morning from the same window.

senses.head: Behold! — presenting something
body: Imperative only, and today usually playful or ironic when a thing is revealed. (вот!, смотрите!)
examples: Behold the size of that canyon.
He opened the box and — behold — the missing part was inside.

senses.head: Lo and behold
body: A frozen phrase introducing a surprise. It is the only place most Americans ever use the verb. (и вот, представьте себе)
examples: We drove all that way and, lo and behold, the museum was closed.
I looked again and, lo and behold, the keys were sitting on the counter.
Nobody who had beheld the wreck could describe it calmly.

entries.register: archaic — literary and ceremonial; alive in speech only in lo and behold
entries.contrast: It follows hold. The verb is literary or ceremonial; in ordinary speech it survives mostly in the fixed phrase lo and behold.
entries.verb type: stative-leaning perception verb, patterning with see rather than watch: the progressive is unnatural — ✗ the crowd is beholding the eclipse. Literary throughout, and imperative-only in Behold the size of that canyon.
entries.transitivity: transitive, with an obligatory object (the crowd beheld the eclipse, few travelers have beheld that valley); the frozen lo and behold takes no object at all.
entries.passive: restricted — possible only in literary register: a sight beheld by few passes, while a full the eclipse was beheld by the crowd reads as costume English.

entries.meaning: To happen to someone, especially to happen badly.
examples: Woe betide the student who forgets that deadline.
Woe betide anyone who touches my coffee.
Woe betides the traveler who ignores that sign.
Whatever may betide, we will meet again in spring.
Great sorrow betid the household that winter.
Stranger things had betid the village before the bridge was built.

senses.head: Woe betide — a warning
body: The one frozen phrase that keeps this verb alive. It is a subjunctive, so it normally takes no ending, though woe betides also turns up. (горе тому, кто...)
examples: Woe betide the student who forgets that deadline.
Woe betide anyone who touches my coffee.
Woe betides the traveler who ignores that sign.

senses.head: Happen, befall
body: Archaic outside of the phrase above; the past betid is museum English. (постигать, случаться (с кем-л.))
examples: Whatever may betide, we will meet again in spring.
Great sorrow betid the household that winter.
Stranger things had betid the village before the bridge was built.

entries.register: archaic — no longer current; one frozen phrase, woe betide, keeps it in the language
entries.third person: betides · -ing form: betiding (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: Archaic. In living American English the verb appears in one frozen phrase, woe betide — a subjunctive, so it takes no ending: Woe betide anyone who is late. The past betid is museum English.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, but an event verb rather than a deed: something befalls a person. Archaic outside the subjunctive woe betide, which takes no ending (woe betide anyone who is late).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the person affected as object (woe betide the student who forgets, great sorrow betid the household), intransitive when the event simply occurs (whatever may betide, we will meet again).
entries.passive: no — the verb is archaic and its object is an experiencer, not a patient: ✗ the household was betid by great sorrow is not English in any register.

entries.meaning: To wait, especially to wait for the right moment.
examples: Bide your time and the price will come down.
She bides her time better than anyone I know.
He bided his time until the market turned.
They have bided their time long enough.
The old sailor bode his time ashore for a year.
He had bode in that harbor town all winter, waiting for a berth.

senses.head: Bide one's time
body: The one living use, and there Americans say bided. Do not confuse it with the separate regular verb bode, to be a sign of something — this bodes well. (выжидать удобного момента)
examples: Bide your time and the price will come down.
She bides her time better than anyone I know.
He bided his time until the market turned.
They have bided their time long enough.

senses.head: Stay, dwell, remain
body: Archaic and dialectal, and the sense that carries the strong forms bode, bode. (оставаться, пребывать)
examples: The old sailor bode his time ashore for a year.
He had bode in that harbor town all winter, waiting for a berth.

entries.register: rare — alive only in bide your time; the strong bode is older still
entries.third person: bides · -ing form: biding (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: The one living use is bide your time, and there Americans say bided: He bided his time. Bode now works mostly as a separate regular verb meaning to be a sign of something — this bodes well, it boded ill — which has its own -d past and is not this verb at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, but alive only inside a fixed frame. Bide one's time is the one living use; do not confuse it with the separate regular verb bode, to be a sign of something (this bodes well).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the living idiom, where the object is fixed and possessive (he bided his time), intransitive in the archaic dwelling sense (he had bode in that harbor town all winter).
entries.passive: no — the idiom's object cannot be promoted: ✗ his time was bided. The dwelling sense is intransitive and has no passive either.

entries.meaning: To tie things together, to place someone under an obligation, or to make separate things hold fast to each other.
examples: We bind the reports in black covers.
She bound the stack of letters with kitchen twine.
Someone has bound all the cables with zip ties.
The contract binds both parties for five years.
He has bound himself to a two-year lease.
The treaty had bound them long before the war started.
Something like this was bound to happen eventually.
We were on a train bound for Chicago.
Shared work binds a crew faster than anything else.
Grief had bound the two families together for good.
That shop still binds dissertations by hand.
They bound my grandfather's letters into a single volume.
Medics bind the wound before they move anyone.
She bound up his arm with a torn shirt.
An egg helps the mixture bind.
The drawer binds whenever the wood swells.
The brake has bound against the rotor since the last repair.
The antibody binds to a protein on the cell surface.
The molecule has bound to the receptor site.
We bound the shortcut to a different key.

senses.head: Tie, fasten together
body: The literal core sense: joining things with rope, twine, wire, or tape. (связывать, завязывать)
examples: We bind the reports in black covers.
She bound the stack of letters with kitchen twine.
Someone has bound all the cables with zip ties.

senses.head: Place under an obligation
body: Legal and contractual, and the reason binding is an adjective in its own right. (обязывать, связывать обязательством)
examples: The contract binds both parties for five years.
He has bound himself to a two-year lease.
The treaty had bound them long before the war started.

senses.head: Be bound to; be bound for
body: Two frozen adjectival uses of the participle: bound to means certain to, and bound for means headed for. Neither behaves like an ordinary passive. (непременно, обязательно; направляющийся (куда-л.))
examples: Something like this was bound to happen eventually.
We were on a train bound for Chicago.

senses.head: Hold together, unite
body: Figurative, of what holds a group or a story together. (сплачивать, объединять)
examples: Shared work binds a crew faster than anything else.
Grief had bound the two families together for good.

senses.head: Bind a book
body: The bookbinding sense; the trade is called binding. (переплетать)
examples: That shop still binds dissertations by hand.
They bound my grandfather's letters into a single volume.

senses.head: Bind a wound; bind up
body: Somewhat formal or biblical; everyday speech says bandage. (перевязывать (рану))
examples: Medics bind the wound before they move anyone.
She bound up his arm with a torn shirt.

senses.head: Hold fast; stick, jam
body: Intransitive, used of a mixture that comes together and of a mechanism that seizes. (схватываться; заедать, заклинивать)
examples: An egg helps the mixture bind.
The drawer binds whenever the wood swells.
The brake has bound against the rotor since the last repair.

senses.head: Bind to (chemistry, computing)
body: Technical, but a learner meets it constantly in science writing and in software documentation. (связываться (с рецептором); привязывать (к порту, ключу))
examples: The antibody binds to a protein on the cell surface.
The molecule has bound to the receptor site.
We bound the shortcut to a different key.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary in speech and writing, and bound to is pure conversation
entries.contrast: Bound is three words at once: this past tense; a regular verb meaning to leap — the dog bounded up the steps; and an adjective meaning headed for — a train bound for Chicago. Only the first is a form of bind.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout. The participle bound has two frozen adjectival lives that are no longer verbal: bound to happen (certain to) and bound for Chicago (headed for).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the tying, obliging, uniting, bookbinding, and dressing senses (she bound the stack of letters, the contract binds both parties), intransitive in the setting and jamming senses (an egg helps the mixture bind, the drawer binds whenever the wood swells).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the letters were bound with kitchen twine, both parties are bound by the contract for five years. No passive of the intransitive the drawer binds, and it was bound to happen is an adjective, not a passive.
entries.phrasal verbs: bind over · bind up

entries.meaning: To lose blood, or to let a fluid drain slowly out of something.
examples: Cuts on the scalp bleed more than they should.
His nose bled for ten minutes.
She had bled through two bandages before the nurse came back.
You have to bleed the brakes after changing the lines.
He bled the radiator to stop the knocking.
The mechanic has bled every line on the car.
The company bleeds cash every quarter.
The fund bled investors for three straight years.
Cheap dye bleeds in hot water.
The red had bled into the collar before she noticed.
Work bleeds into the weekend if you let it.
The two chapters have bled into each other.
My heart bleeds for anyone driving in this.
We bled for that family when the story came out.

senses.head: Lose blood
body: The literal sense. Never the regular form — the past is always bled. (кровоточить, истекать кровью)
examples: Cuts on the scalp bleed more than they should.
His nose bled for ten minutes.
She had bled through two bandages before the nurse came back.

senses.head: Bleed a line, drain fluid
body: Transitive and technical: bleed the brakes, bleed a radiator. It keeps the strong form too. (спускать (воздух, жидкость), прокачивать)
examples: You have to bleed the brakes after changing the lines.
He bled the radiator to stop the knocking.
The mechanic has bled every line on the car.

senses.head: Lose money steadily
body: Business writing, either intransitive or with cash as the object. (терять деньги, истекать деньгами)
examples: The company bleeds cash every quarter.
The fund bled investors for three straight years.

senses.head: Run, spread (of color or ink)
body: Of dye in the wash and of ink on paper. (растекаться, расплываться (о краске))
examples: Cheap dye bleeds in hot water.
The red had bled into the collar before she noticed.

senses.head: Bleed into — blur together
body: Figurative, of boundaries that fail to hold. (перетекать, сливаться (одно в другое))
examples: Work bleeds into the weekend if you let it.
The two chapters have bled into each other.

senses.head: One's heart bleeds
body: A fixed sympathy phrase, and in American speech usually sarcastic. (сердце обливается кровью, всей душой сочувствовать)
examples: My heart bleeds for anyone driving in this.
We bled for that family when the story came out.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary American, literal and figurative alike
entries.contrast: The vowel shortens and the spelling loses a letter with it: bleed has two e's, bled has one, and ✗ bleeded is never right. The same shortening runs through feed, breed and lead. The transitive sense keeps the strong form too — he bled the brakes, not ✗ he bleeded the brakes.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a process verb literally (his nose bled) and figuratively (the company bleeds cash).
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in the losing-blood, spreading, and blurring senses (cheap dye bleeds in hot water, work bleeds into the weekend), transitive in the draining and financial senses (he bled the radiator, the fund bled investors for three years).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — every line on the car has been bled, the brakes were bled after the lines were changed. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ ten minutes were bled by his nose.
entries.phrasal verbs: bleed dry · bleed off · bleed out

entries.meaning: To feed a baby with milk from the breast.
examples: Many mothers breastfeed for the first six months.
She breastfed both of her children.
They have breastfed longer than the pediatrician expected.
My sister breastfeeds in public without a second thought.
Breastfed infants show a different gut flora.
By the time the twins were weaned she had breastfed for two solid years.

senses.head: Nurse a baby
body: Used with or without an object: you can breastfeed a baby or simply breastfeed. (кормить грудью)
examples: Many mothers breastfeed for the first six months.
She breastfed both of her children.
They have breastfed longer than the pediatrician expected.
My sister breastfeeds in public without a second thought.

senses.head: Breastfed — raised on breast milk
body: The participle used as an adjective, common in medical and parenting writing. (вскормленный грудью)
examples: Breastfed infants show a different gut flora.
By the time the twins were weaned she had breastfed for two solid years.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary in any conversation about babies
entries.contrast: It follows feed.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic. The participle also serves as a plain adjective in medical and parenting writing: breastfed infants show a different gut flora.
entries.transitivity: both — the object is optional: transitive with the baby as object (she breastfed both of her children), intransitive when the activity alone is meant (many mothers breastfeed for the first six months).
entries.passive: yes — both children were breastfed for two solid years, the twins had been breastfed until they were weaned.

entries.meaning: To produce offspring, to raise animals or plants for chosen traits, or to give rise to something.
examples: They bred quarter horses on that farm for sixty years.
The kennel breeds only two litters a year.
Those roses had been bred for cold winters.
Rabbits breed fast.
The herons have bred on that island for decades.
Familiarity has bred a certain carelessness around here.
Delay breeds rumor.
The shortage bred a black market almost overnight.
He was born and bred in Tulsa.
That caution had been bred into her since childhood.

senses.head: Raise selectively, develop a strain
body: Transitive, of animals and plants bred toward a purpose. (разводить, выводить (породу, сорт))
examples: They bred quarter horses on that farm for sixty years.
The kennel breeds only two litters a year.
Those roses had been bred for cold winters.

senses.head: Reproduce, have young
body: Intransitive, and used of animals rather than people. (размножаться, плодиться)
examples: Rabbits breed fast.
The herons have bred on that island for decades.

senses.head: Give rise to, produce
body: Figurative, of conditions producing feelings or behavior. The proverb is familiarity breeds contempt. (порождать, вызывать)
examples: Familiarity has bred a certain carelessness around here.
Delay breeds rumor.
The shortage bred a black market almost overnight.

senses.head: Bring up, raise (a person)
body: Now almost only in fixed phrases: born and bred, bred in the bone, well-bred. The past bred is a homophone of bread, which is where the misspelling comes from. (воспитывать, растить)
examples: He was born and bred in Tulsa.
That caution had been bred into her since childhood.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary American, of animals and of trouble alike
entries.contrast: The past bred is a homophone of bread, which is where the misspelling ✗ home-bread comes from. The verb is bred, always.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, causative when a breeder is behind it (they bred quarter horses) and simply eventive when the animals do it themselves (rabbits breed fast).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the selective-breeding, causing, and raising senses (the kennel breeds only two litters a year, delay breeds rumor), intransitive in the reproducing sense (the herons have bred on that island for decades).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — those roses had been bred for cold winters, he was born and bred in Tulsa. No passive of the intransitive rabbits breed fast.

entries.meaning: To scold someone mildly.
examples: She chides me whenever I skip breakfast.
Do not chide him for a mistake he did not make.
The teacher chid the class for its sloppy handwriting.
He has chid his brother about that car a hundred times.
Their mother had chid them into silence before the guests arrived.
She chided him out of buying the thing at all.

senses.head: Scold, reproach gently
body: Formal and a little literary. Modern American English makes it regular — chided, chided — and the strong chid and chidden now read as archaic. (бранить, укорять)
examples: She chides me whenever I skip breakfast.
Do not chide him for a mistake he did not make.
The teacher chid the class for its sloppy handwriting.
He has chid his brother about that car a hundred times.

senses.head: Chide someone into silence
body: The verb takes a direction: scolding used to move someone toward or away from an action. (укорами добиться чего-л. от кого-л.)
examples: Their mother had chid them into silence before the guests arrived.
She chided him out of buying the thing at all.

entries.register: formal — journalistic and literary; ordinary speech says scold
entries.third person: chides · -ing form: chiding (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: In modern American English the verb is regular: chide, chided, chided. The old forms chid and chidden now read as archaic.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a speech-act verb, formal and journalistic where ordinary speech says scold.
entries.transitivity: transitive, with the person scolded as object (she chides me whenever I skip breakfast); the reason and the result follow prepositions (chide him for a mistake, chided him out of buying the thing).
entries.passive: yes — he was chided for a mistake he did not make, the class was chided for its sloppy handwriting. Modern American writes the passive with the regular chided, not ✗ was chid.

entries.meaning: To go up something using hands and feet, or simply to rise.
examples: We climb that ridge every Fourth of July.
She climbs like she was born on a rock wall.
He clumb that fence quicker than a cat.
They had clumb halfway up the water tower before anybody hollered.
Prices climb every summer.
The temperature has climbed six degrees since noon.
He climbed into the truck without a word.
She has climbed in and out of that attic all morning.
She climbed from clerk to partner in nine years.
The song has climbed to number three.
Ivy climbs the whole north wall.
The road climbs for six miles after the bridge.
The plane climbs to cruising altitude in about twelve minutes.
We had climbed to thirty thousand feet before the seatbelt sign went off.

senses.head: Go up using hands and feet
body: The core sense. Standard American English is regular here — climb, climbed, climbed; clumb is a dialect past you meet in Twain and in older Southern and Appalachian speech, never in edited prose. (карабкаться, взбираться, лазить)
examples: We climb that ridge every Fourth of July.
She climbs like she was born on a rock wall.
He clumb that fence quicker than a cat.
They had clumb halfway up the water tower before anybody hollered.

senses.head: Rise, increase
body: Of any measured quantity going up steadily. (расти, подниматься (о ценах, температуре))
examples: Prices climb every summer.
The temperature has climbed six degrees since noon.

senses.head: Climb into, climb out of
body: Always with a preposition: climb into bed, climb out of a truck, climb through a window. (залезать, вылезать)
examples: He climbed into the truck without a word.
She has climbed in and out of that attic all morning.

senses.head: Rise in rank or standing
body: Figurative, and usually with a ladder or a chart in the picture. (продвигаться (по служебной лестнице))
examples: She climbed from clerk to partner in nine years.
The song has climbed to number three.

senses.head: Slope or grow upward
body: Of plants that grow up a support and of roads that rise. (виться вверх; идти в гору)
examples: Ivy climbs the whole north wall.
The road climbs for six miles after the bridge.

senses.head: Gain altitude (of an aircraft)
body: Aviation, intransitive. (набирать высоту)
examples: The plane climbs to cruising altitude in about twelve minutes.
We had climbed to thirty thousand feet before the seatbelt sign went off.

entries.register: everyday — the verb is ordinary; only the dialect past clumb is not
entries.third person: climbs · -ing form: climbing (the b stays silent)
entries.contrast: Standard American English is regular: climb, climbed, climbed. Clumb is a dialect past — you meet it in Twain and in older Appalachian and Southern speech, never in edited prose.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a motion verb literally (we climb that ridge) and a change-of-degree verb figuratively (prices climb every summer).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the thing scaled as object (ivy climbs the whole north wall), intransitive in the rising, aviation, and preposition-taking senses (the temperature has climbed six degrees, he climbed into the truck).
entries.passive: restricted — natural only when the object is a genuine climbing objective: that face has been climbed only twice. The rising senses have no passive at all: ✗ six degrees have been climbed by the temperature.

entries.meaning: To hold on tightly, or to stick to a surface.
examples: The toddler clung to her father's leg.
She had clung to the railing until the ferry steadied.
Climbers cling to that wall with their fingertips.
Wet leaves cling to the windshield.
Static clings to everything in this dry air.
The campfire smell has clung to that coat for a week.
He has clung to that theory for thirty years.
They clung to the hope that the flight would be rerouted.
He clings to whoever pays him attention.
The puppy clung to us for a solid week.

senses.head: Hold on tightly
body: Physical grip, usually out of fear or need. There is no form clinged. (цепляться, крепко держаться)
examples: The toddler clung to her father's leg.
She had clung to the railing until the ferry steadied.
Climbers cling to that wall with their fingertips.

senses.head: Stick to a surface
body: Of wet, static, or smelly things that will not come off. (прилипать, липнуть)
examples: Wet leaves cling to the windshield.
Static clings to everything in this dry air.
The campfire smell has clung to that coat for a week.

senses.head: Cling to a belief
body: Figurative, and it usually implies the thing is not worth holding. (цепляться (за идею, надежду, власть))
examples: He has clung to that theory for thirty years.
They clung to the hope that the flight would be rerouted.

senses.head: Cling to a person
body: Emotional dependence, and the source of the adjective clingy. (льнуть, не отходить ни на шаг)
examples: He clings to whoever pays him attention.
The puppy clung to us for a solid week.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary American, of static, toddlers, and beliefs
entries.contrast: Clung covers both the past and the participle, and ✗ clinged is not English. Keep the verb apart from the adjective clingy and from British cling film, which Americans call plastic wrap; neither is a form of the verb.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic but durative: it describes holding on over time rather than a single act, physically (the toddler clung to her leg), adhesively (static clings to everything), or figuratively (he has clung to that theory for thirty years).
entries.transitivity: intransitive in every sense — what is held onto always follows to or another preposition: ✗ she clung the railing, only she clung to the railing.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so there is no object to promote: ✗ the railing was clung. Even the prepositional passive is marginal: ? that theory has been clung to for thirty years.
entries.phrasal verbs: cling on · cling to
entries.see also: fling, sling, sting, string, swing, wring

entries.meaning: To breed two different varieties or species together.
examples: Growers crossbreed these apples for firmness.
The lab crossbred the two strains last spring.
Ranchers have crossbred Angus and Hereford cattle for generations.
The two populations crossbreed wherever their ranges overlap.
Domestic cats and wildcats have crossbred in that valley for centuries.
The show crossbreeds a courtroom drama with a sitcom.
Someone had crossbred a pickup and a sports car and called it innovation.

senses.head: Breed two varieties together
body: Transitive, and deliberate — the work of a breeder or a lab. (скрещивать (породы, сорта))
examples: Growers crossbreed these apples for firmness.
The lab crossbred the two strains last spring.
Ranchers have crossbred Angus and Hereford cattle for generations.

senses.head: Breed across a line naturally
body: Intransitive, with no breeder involved. (скрещиваться (в природе))
examples: The two populations crossbreed wherever their ranges overlap.
Domestic cats and wildcats have crossbred in that valley for centuries.

senses.head: Blend two unlike things
body: Figurative, of genres, designs, or ideas spliced together. (смешивать, скрещивать (перен.))
examples: The show crossbreeds a courtroom drama with a sitcom.
Someone had crossbred a pickup and a sports car and called it innovation.

entries.register: rare — a breeder's and a biologist's word; ordinary speech says cross or mix
entries.contrast: It follows breed.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, causative when a breeder or a lab is behind it and eventive when populations mix on their own.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the varieties as object (the lab crossbred the two strains, growers crossbreed these apples for firmness), intransitive when it happens without a breeder (the two populations crossbreed wherever their ranges overlap).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — Angus and Hereford cattle have been crossbred for generations, the two strains were crossbred last spring. No passive of the intransitive.

entries.meaning: To break up and move earth, or to make a hole in something.
examples: They dig a new well every few years.
The dog dug under the fence again.
Crews have dug three feet down and hit rock.
She dug out the old lease from a box in the garage.
Reporters have dug up three more emails.
He digs through the archive whenever he needs a story.
The committee has dug into the contracts line by line.
Dig in before it gets cold.
The troops had dug in along the ridge.
He dug in his heels and refused to sign.
The strap digs into my shoulder.
She dug an elbow into my ribs to shut me up.
She digs at him about the car every chance she gets.
He has dug at me about that trip all week.
I dig that record.
He dug the whole album the first time he heard it.

senses.head: Excavate, make a hole
body: The literal core sense, of people, animals, and machines. (копать, рыть)
examples: They dig a new well every few years.
The dog dug under the fence again.
Crews have dug three feet down and hit rock.

senses.head: Dig up, dig out — unearth
body: Literal for potatoes and fossils, figurative for old records and old grudges. (выкапывать, откапывать, раскопать)
examples: She dug out the old lease from a box in the garage.
Reporters have dug up three more emails.

senses.head: Dig into — investigate
body: Figurative, of research and scrutiny. (копаться, разбираться (в чём-л.))
examples: He digs through the archive whenever he needs a story.
The committee has dug into the contracts line by line.

senses.head: Dig in — start eating; entrench
body: Two related uses of the same phrasal: an invitation to eat, and a refusal to move. Dig in your heels is the stubborn one. (приниматься за еду; окапываться, упереться)
examples: Dig in before it gets cold.
The troops had dug in along the ridge.
He dug in his heels and refused to sign.

senses.head: Press or poke into
body: Of something hard pressing against the body. (втыкать, вонзать, впиваться)
examples: The strap digs into my shoulder.
She dug an elbow into my ribs to shut me up.

senses.head: Take a jab at someone
body: Usually dig at; the noun a dig is commoner than the verb. (подкалывать, поддевать)
examples: She digs at him about the car every chance she gets.
He has dug at me about that trip all week.

senses.head: Like, appreciate (slang)
body: Dated American slang out of the 1950s and 1960s, and still perfectly understood. It takes the same strong forms. (врубаться, тащиться (сленг))
examples: I dig that record.
He dug the whole album the first time he heard it.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: The slang sense, to like something, takes the same forms: I dug that record.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic. The 1950s slang sense of liking something (I dig that record) is stative in meaning, but unlike most statives it takes the progressive freely: I'm digging this album.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the hole or the unearthed thing as object (they dig a new well, she dug out the old lease), intransitive when the digging alone is meant or a preposition follows (the dog dug under the fence, the committee has dug into the contracts).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the well was dug in 1954, three more emails have been dug up. The slang liking sense refuses it: ✗ that record is dug by me.
entries.phrasal verbs: dig in · dig into · dig out · dig up

entries.meaning: To make a short ringing sound, to put a small dent in something, or to knock someone down a peg.
examples: I dinged the car door in the parking garage.
Somebody has dinged every corner of that table.
The elevator dings at every floor.
Timers ding all over the kitchen at six.
The bell dung twice and fell silent.
That old clock has dung the hour since my grandfather's time.
The graders ding you for skipping the citations.
Three schools dinged him before he got an offer.
Something had dung against the hull in the night.
Hail dinged the roof of the shed all afternoon.

senses.head: Dent, chip, nick
body: The commonest modern American use, above all of cars. Always regular here: dinged. (поцарапать, помять, стукнуть)
examples: I dinged the car door in the parking garage.
Somebody has dinged every corner of that table.

senses.head: Ring, chime
body: The original sense, and the one that once took the strong forms. Dung is now archaic and dialectal, and it collides with the plain noun dung, meaning manure. (звенеть, звякать)
examples: The elevator dings at every floor.
Timers ding all over the kitchen at six.
The bell dung twice and fell silent.
That old clock has dung the hour since my grandfather's time.

senses.head: Penalize, mark down, reject
body: Informal American, common in grading, hiring, and admissions. (снижать оценку; отсеивать (разг.))
examples: The graders ding you for skipping the citations.
Three schools dinged him before he got an offer.

senses.head: Strike a light blow
body: The oldest sense, now archaic on its own but audible behind the dent sense. (стукнуть, ударить)
examples: Something had dung against the hull in the night.
Hail dinged the roof of the shed all afternoon.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary American for denting a car or rejecting an applicant
entries.contrast: In ordinary American English this verb is regular — dinged, dinged — in both the ringing sense and the common everyday sense of putting a small dent in something: I dinged the car door. The strong past dung is archaic and dialectal, and it collides with the plain noun dung, meaning manure.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a sound verb in the original sense (the elevator dings at every floor) and an impact verb in the modern American one (I dinged the car door).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the denting, penalizing, and striking senses (three schools dinged him, hail dinged the roof), intransitive in the ringing sense (timers ding all over the kitchen at six).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — he was dinged by three schools before he got an offer, every corner of that table has been dinged. No passive of the ringing sense: ✗ the hour was dung by the clock.

entries.meaning: To give food to a person or animal, or to supply something steadily.
examples: We feed the cats at six.
She has fed that stray all winter.
They had fed the whole crowd before the speeches started.
Deer feed at dusk.
The larvae feed on the underside of the leaf.
Bats had fed on the insects around the lamp all night.
The river feeds three reservoirs.
Two sensors feed data to the controller.
That one server has fed the whole network since Tuesday.
He fed the parking meter another quarter.
Feed the sheet in face down.
The rumor feeds on every denial.
The fire had fed on dry brush for two days.
That job feeds a family of five.
He fed four kids on a mechanic's wages.
I am fed up with the noise.
They had long been fed up with the delays.
The point guard feeds the post all night.
She fed him a perfect ball at the far post.

senses.head: Give food to
body: The core transitive sense. (кормить)
examples: We feed the cats at six.
She has fed that stray all winter.
They had fed the whole crowd before the speeches started.

senses.head: Eat, graze (of animals)
body: Intransitive, and used of animals rather than people; often feed on. (питаться, кормиться)
examples: Deer feed at dusk.
The larvae feed on the underside of the leaf.
Bats had fed on the insects around the lamp all night.

senses.head: Supply steadily
body: Of rivers, wires, and data streams — anything that keeps something else running. (питать, снабжать, подавать)
examples: The river feeds three reservoirs.
Two sensors feed data to the controller.
That one server has fed the whole network since Tuesday.

senses.head: Feed a meter, feed in
body: Feeding a meter, a printer, or a machine that takes material piece by piece. (вставлять, подавать, скармливать (по частям))
examples: He fed the parking meter another quarter.
Feed the sheet in face down.

senses.head: Feed on, feed off
body: Figurative, of things that grow on what should have stopped them. (подпитываться, кормиться (чем-л.))
examples: The rumor feeds on every denial.
The fire had fed on dry brush for two days.

senses.head: Support financially
body: A family or a household is the object. (содержать, кормить (семью))
examples: That job feeds a family of five.
He fed four kids on a mechanic's wages.

senses.head: Be fed up
body: A fixed adjectival participle, always fed up, usually fed up with. It is never active — you cannot feed someone up in this sense. (быть сытым по горло, надоесть)
examples: I am fed up with the noise.
They had long been fed up with the delays.

senses.head: Pass the ball (sports)
body: Sports commentary, with the receiving player as object. (отдавать пас, снабжать мячом)
examples: The point guard feeds the post all night.
She fed him a perfect ball at the far post.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: The participle also lives inside a fixed adjective: fed up, meaning out of patience — I am fed up with the noise.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from nourishing to supplying (two sensors feed data to the controller). Fed up is a frozen adjectival participle, not a live verb form.
entries.transitivity: all three — intransitive of animals grazing (deer feed at dusk), transitive with the eater or the machine as object (we feed the cats at six, he fed the parking meter), and ditransitive in the supplying and sports senses (she fed him a perfect ball, two sensors feed the controller data).
entries.passive: yes — the whole crowd had been fed before the speeches started, that stray has been fed all winter. But I am fed up with the noise only looks passive: there is no active ✗ the noise fed me up.
entries.phrasal verbs: feed back · feed into · feed off · feed on · feed up
entries.see also: breastfeed, force-feed, overfeed, breed, bleed, speed

entries.meaning: To take part in a struggle, physical or otherwise.
examples: He fought in the Pacific.
Two guys fight outside that bar every weekend.
The champion has fought twice this year.
They fight about money every January.
We fought the whole drive home.
Crews fought the fire for nine days.
She has fought the same infection three times.
We had fought the rezoning for two years before the vote.
The union has fought three contract battles this decade.
She fights every claim the insurer denies.
He fought the ticket and won.
She fought back and the whole thing stopped.
Consumers have fought back with a boycott.
He fought off a cold all week.
The company has fought off two takeover attempts.
We fought our way through the crowd.
They had fought their way into the semifinals.

senses.head: Fight physically; wage war
body: The literal sense, from a schoolyard scuffle to a war. The past is spelled fought, one of the -ought family with bought and brought. (драться, сражаться, воевать)
examples: He fought in the Pacific.
Two guys fight outside that bar every weekend.
The champion has fought twice this year.

senses.head: Quarrel, argue
body: No blows involved; usually fight about or fight over something. (ссориться, ругаться)
examples: They fight about money every January.
We fought the whole drive home.

senses.head: Struggle against something
body: The object is a problem rather than a person: a fire, an illness, the traffic. (бороться (с болезнью, пожаром, стихией))
examples: Crews fought the fire for nine days.
She has fought the same infection three times.

senses.head: Campaign for or against
body: Political and civic, of long public efforts. (отстаивать, бороться за/против)
examples: We had fought the rezoning for two years before the vote.
The union has fought three contract battles this decade.

senses.head: Contest legally
body: American usage lets you fight a ticket, fight a claim, or fight a will. (оспаривать (в суде), опротестовывать)
examples: She fights every claim the insurer denies.
He fought the ticket and won.

senses.head: Fight back
body: To resist after being attacked; also fight back tears, meaning to hold them in. (давать отпор, сопротивляться)
examples: She fought back and the whole thing stopped.
Consumers have fought back with a boycott.

senses.head: Fight off
body: To repel something coming at you — attackers, a cold, sleep. (отбиваться, побороть (болезнь, нападение))
examples: He fought off a cold all week.
The company has fought off two takeover attempts.

senses.head: Fight one's way
body: Movement achieved by effort, literal or figurative. (пробиваться, прокладывать себе путь)
examples: We fought our way through the crowd.
They had fought their way into the semifinals.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: The past is spelled fought, one of the -ought family along with bought and brought. ✗ fighted and ✗ faught are never right.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a verb of struggle, literal (he fought in the Pacific), interpersonal (they fight about money), and civic (the union has fought three contract battles).
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive when no opponent is named or one follows a preposition (two guys fight outside that bar, we fought the whole drive home), transitive with an opponent, an obstacle, or a claim as object (crews fought the fire, he fought the ticket and won).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the fire was fought for nine days, the rezoning had been fought for two years. No passive of the quarreling sense: ✗ money is fought about by them.
entries.phrasal verbs: fight back · fight down · fight off · fight out

entries.meaning: To come upon something, to discover it after looking, or to form a judgment about it.
examples: She found my keys in the freezer.
We had found the leak before the plumber arrived.
Investigators have found no evidence of tampering.
He finds good bookstores wherever he goes.
She found a twenty in an old coat.
Researchers found that the effect disappears after a year.
We have found the opposite to be true.
I find the whole argument unconvincing.
She found the class harder than she expected.
The jury found him guilty on two counts.
The court has found for the plaintiff.
We found ourselves in the wrong terminal.
He has found himself out of work twice this year.
I cannot find the time to read anything.
They found the money somewhere.
Find out what it costs before you sign anything.
She had found out about the transfer from a coworker.
Water finds its level.
The shot found the top corner.

senses.head: Discover after searching
body: The core sense: you were looking, and there it was. (находить, отыскивать)
examples: She found my keys in the freezer.
We had found the leak before the plumber arrived.
Investigators have found no evidence of tampering.

senses.head: Come upon by chance
body: No searching implied — the thing simply turned up. (натыкаться, обнаруживать случайно)
examples: He finds good bookstores wherever he goes.
She found a twenty in an old coat.

senses.head: Learn, establish as a fact
body: Research and reporting, usually find that. (выяснять, устанавливать)
examples: Researchers found that the effect disappears after a year.
We have found the opposite to be true.

senses.head: Consider, judge to be
body: Takes an object plus a description: find it odd, find him difficult, find the class hard. (находить, считать (каким-л.))
examples: I find the whole argument unconvincing.
She found the class harder than she expected.

senses.head: Return a verdict (law)
body: Legal: a jury finds someone guilty, and a court finds for one side. (признавать (виновным), выносить решение)
examples: The jury found him guilty on two counts.
The court has found for the plaintiff.

senses.head: Find oneself in a situation
body: Reflexive, and it says the situation was not planned. (оказаться, очутиться)
examples: We found ourselves in the wrong terminal.
He has found himself out of work twice this year.

senses.head: Manage to get (time, money, words)
body: The object is a resource that had to be produced from somewhere. (выкраивать, изыскивать)
examples: I cannot find the time to read anything.
They found the money somewhere.

senses.head: Find out
body: Phrasal, of learning a fact — often one somebody was hiding. (узнавать, выяснять)
examples: Find out what it costs before you sign anything.
She had found out about the transfer from a coworker.

senses.head: Reach, arrive at (of a thing)
body: The subject is inanimate and gets where it naturally goes: water finds its level, the shot found the corner. (достигать, попадать (в цель))
examples: Water finds its level.
The shot found the top corner.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Found is also a separate regular verb meaning to establish: They founded the college in 1851. So the college was founded in 1851 (set up) says something quite different from the college was found in 1851 (located).
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the discovery senses (she found my keys in the freezer); stative in the judging sense, which reports an opinion rather than an act — I find the whole argument unconvincing, and the progressive is odd there: ✗ I am finding the argument unconvincing.
entries.transitivity: transitive throughout, with an obligatory object (✗ she found is incomplete); senses 4 and 5 add an object complement (I find the argument unconvincing, the jury found him guilty on two counts), and find someone the time also allows two objects.
entries.passive: yes — no evidence of tampering has been found, he was found guilty on two counts, the effect was found to disappear after a year. Even the stative judging sense passivizes: the argument was found unconvincing.
entries.phrasal verbs: find for · find out

entries.meaning: To throw something hard or carelessly.
examples: Don't fling your coat on the floor.
Someone had flung a rock through the front window.
The pitcher flings it past the batter every time.
He flung the door open and walked out.
She has flung her arms around every person in the room.
She has flung herself into the new job.
He flung himself into the campaign the day after the funeral.
He flings off his boots the second he gets home.
They had flung away a two-goal lead.

senses.head: Throw hard or carelessly
body: The core sense, with force or with indifference behind it. There is no form flinged. (швырять, бросать, метать)
examples: Don't fling your coat on the floor.
Someone had flung a rock through the front window.
The pitcher flings it past the batter every time.

senses.head: Move abruptly, throw open
body: Of doors, arms, and heads moved with a single violent motion. (распахивать; резко вскинуть)
examples: He flung the door open and walked out.
She has flung her arms around every person in the room.

senses.head: Fling oneself into something
body: Reflexive and figurative: to commit all your energy at once. (с головой уйти во что-л.)
examples: She has flung herself into the new job.
He flung himself into the campaign the day after the funeral.

senses.head: Fling off, fling away
body: To discard abruptly — clothes literally, an advantage figuratively. (сбрасывать; отбрасывать, разбазаривать)
examples: He flings off his boots the second he gets home.
They had flung away a two-goal lead.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary American; flung comes out without hesitation
entries.contrast: Flung is the only past — ✗ flinged does not exist. The noun a fling, a brief romance or a spree, is the same word but takes a regular plural: two flings, never ✗ two flung.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a verb of forceful motion, whether the force is anger, haste, or indifference (he flung the door open and walked out).
entries.transitivity: transitive, with an obligatory object (don't fling your coat on the floor; ✗ don't fling), and reflexive in the commitment sense (she has flung herself into the new job).
entries.passive: yes in the ordinary transitive sense — a rock had been flung through the front window, a two-goal lead had been flung away. The reflexive use has none: ✗ herself was flung into the new job.
entries.see also: cling, sling, sting, string, swing, wring

entries.meaning: To light a large area with broad, powerful lamps.
examples: Crews floodlight the field for night games.
They floodlit the bridge for the anniversary.
Organizers have floodlit the plaza every December since 1998.
The city floodlights the courthouse on holidays.
The stadium had been floodlit long before kickoff.
We walked back across a floodlit parking lot.

senses.head: Light a large area
body: Of fields, monuments, and building fronts. Like light, it allows a regular floodlighted, but floodlit is the usual choice. (освещать прожекторами)
examples: Crews floodlight the field for night games.
They floodlit the bridge for the anniversary.
Organizers have floodlit the plaza every December since 1998.
The city floodlights the courthouse on holidays.

senses.head: Floodlit — bathed in floodlight
body: The participle as an adjective, above all in front of a noun: a floodlit field. (залитый светом прожекторов)
examples: The stadium had been floodlit long before kickoff.
We walked back across a floodlit parking lot.

entries.register: rare — stadium and stage lighting; the participle floodlit is what people actually meet
entries.contrast: It follows light, and like light it also allows a regular floodlighted. Floodlit is the usual choice, above all in front of a noun: a floodlit field.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a causative lighting verb. The participle floodlit also works as a plain adjective: a floodlit field, a floodlit parking lot.
entries.transitivity: transitive only, and the object is obligatory — they floodlit the bridge for the anniversary; ✗ crews floodlight is incomplete.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is the usual form — the stadium had been floodlit long before kickoff, the plaza has been floodlit every December since 1998.

entries.meaning: To make a person or animal eat, or to push something on someone who does not want it.
examples: Hospitals force-feed patients only as a last resort.
The vet force-fed the puppy for three days.
They had force-fed the calf until it could nurse on its own.
Advertisers have force-fed us the same jingle all month.
He force-feeds his students dates and names.

senses.head: Make someone eat
body: The literal sense, from medicine, veterinary care, and prisons. It keeps its hyphen in American writing. (кормить насильно)
examples: Hospitals force-feed patients only as a last resort.
The vet force-fed the puppy for three days.
They had force-fed the calf until it could nurse on its own.

senses.head: Push information on someone
body: Figurative, usually with a note of resentment about advertising or rote teaching. (навязывать, вдалбливать)
examples: Advertisers have force-fed us the same jingle all month.
He force-feeds his students dates and names.

entries.register: neutral — plain but narrow; mostly of animals and, figuratively, of ideas
entries.contrast: It follows feed, and it keeps its hyphen in American writing.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and causative: it makes someone take in food, or figuratively information they did not ask for (he force-feeds his students dates and names).
entries.transitivity: transitive, and ditransitive in the figurative sense with both a recipient and a thing (advertisers have force-fed us the same jingle); the literal sense takes one object (the vet force-fed the puppy).
entries.passive: yes — the calf had been force-fed until it could nurse on its own, we have been force-fed the same jingle all month.

entries.meaning: To obtain or receive something, to become something, or to arrive somewhere — the hardest-working verb in English.
examples: I get the mail around noon.
She got a raise in March.
He has gotten three offers this month.
This gets complicated fast.
It got dark before we found the car.
The weather has gotten worse since Tuesday.
What time do you get to work?
We had gotten halfway to Reno before the tire blew.
Get me a chair, would you?
He got his sister from the airport.
I get it now.
Nobody got the joke.
She has never gotten my sense of humor.
Everyone in the office got the flu.
She has gotten strep twice this winter.
I could not get him to sign anything.
We got the roof fixed in October.
She has gotten the whole team to show up early.
I have got a spare key in the car.
She has got two brothers in Denver.
You have got to see this.
He has got to stop doing that.
They got married in a courthouse.
Two people got hurt in the pileup.
Nobody has gotten fired over it yet.
I get up at five.
He had gotten up before the alarm.
She never quite got over it.
He has gotten over the worst of the jet lag.
They get by on one income.
We got by with a rental for a month.
The two of them get along fine.
He has never gotten along with his landlord.

senses.head: Obtain, receive
body: The core sense. American English uses gotten for the participle here: I have gotten three offers, not I have got three offers. (получать, доставать)
examples: I get the mail around noon.
She got a raise in March.
He has gotten three offers this month.

senses.head: Become something
body: With an adjective: get tired, get dark, get better. The commonest way English says that a state is changing. (становиться, делаться)
examples: This gets complicated fast.
It got dark before we found the car.
The weather has gotten worse since Tuesday.

senses.head: Arrive, reach a place
body: Always with a preposition or home: get to work, get there, get home. (добираться, доезжать, попадать)
examples: What time do you get to work?
We had gotten halfway to Reno before the tire blew.

senses.head: Fetch, go and bring
body: Transitive, often with two objects: get me a chair. (принести, сходить за)
examples: Get me a chair, would you?
He got his sister from the airport.

senses.head: Understand, get it
body: Informal but universal in speech: I get it, nobody got the joke. (понимать, доходить (разг.))
examples: I get it now.
Nobody got the joke.
She has never gotten my sense of humor.

senses.head: Catch an illness
body: The everyday alternative to contract. (подхватить, заболеть)
examples: Everyone in the office got the flu.
She has gotten strep twice this winter.

senses.head: Cause, persuade, arrange
body: Two patterns: get someone to do something (persuade) and get something done (arrange for it). (заставить, уговорить; сделать (чужими руками))
examples: I could not get him to sign anything.
We got the roof fixed in October.
She has gotten the whole team to show up early.

senses.head: Have got — possess
body: Present-tense possession, not a perfect at all: I've got a car simply means I have one. This is the one place American English keeps got rather than gotten. (иметь (разг.))
examples: I have got a spare key in the car.
She has got two brothers in Denver.

senses.head: Have got to — must
body: Obligation, spoken far more than written, and often reduced to gotta. Again got, never gotten. (должен, нужно (разг.))
examples: You have got to see this.
He has got to stop doing that.

senses.head: Get + past participle (passive)
body: An informal passive that stresses the event rather than the state: get hired, get married, get hurt. (оказаться, стать (страдательный оборот))
examples: They got married in a courthouse.
Two people got hurt in the pileup.
Nobody has gotten fired over it yet.

senses.head: Get up
body: To rise from bed or from a seat. (вставать, подниматься)
examples: I get up at five.
He had gotten up before the alarm.

senses.head: Get over
body: To recover from an illness, a shock, or a person. (оправиться, пережить, забыть)
examples: She never quite got over it.
He has gotten over the worst of the jet lag.

senses.head: Get by
body: To manage on barely enough. (перебиваться, справляться, обходиться)
examples: They get by on one income.
We got by with a rental for a month.

senses.head: Get along with
body: To have an easy relationship with someone; also get along on its own for managing. (ладить, уживаться)
examples: The two of them get along fine.
He has never gotten along with his landlord.

entries.register: everyday — one of the commonest verbs in the language
entries.contrast: The one place where American and British English part company hardest. The normal American participle is gotten — I have gotten three offers, the weather has gotten worse. Got survives as a participle in two fixed patterns that mean something else: have got for possession (I've got a car) and have got to for obligation (You've got to see this). British English uses got everywhere and finds gotten strange. The forms listed above follow the source list, which is British; in American writing, reach for gotten.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the obtaining, fetching, and arriving senses; linking (copular) with an adjective, where it means become (it got dark, the weather has gotten worse); auxiliary-like in the informal passive get hired, get married, get hurt; and stative in have got (possession) and have got to (obligation), which are present-tense idioms, not perfects.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the obtaining, understanding, and catching senses (she got a raise, nobody got the joke), ditransitive in get me a chair, and intransitive or linking with an adjective, particle, or preposition (it got dark, we had gotten halfway to Reno, they get by on one income).
entries.passive: restricted — get itself barely passivizes: ✗ a raise was gotten by her, and the possessive idiom refuses outright, ✗ a spare key is had got by me. What get actually does is build other verbs' passives: they got married in a courthouse, two people got hurt in the pileup.

entries.meaning: To crush something into powder, or to rub two hard surfaces against each other.
examples: I grind the beans right before brewing.
She ground pepper over the entire plate.
Someone has ground coffee into the carpet.
The mill grinds corn for the whole county.
He grinds his teeth in his sleep.
The gears ground every time he shifted.
That shop grinds lenses to order.
They had ground the blade down to almost nothing.
Traffic had ground to a stop by seven.
The whole project ground to a halt in April.
The commute grinds people down.
Six months of this has ground him down.
She grinds away at the same problem for weeks.
He has ground out four hundred pages of the thing.

senses.head: Crush into powder
body: Coffee, grain, pepper, meat. The past ground is spelled exactly like the noun ground, the earth. (молоть, перемалывать)
examples: I grind the beans right before brewing.
She ground pepper over the entire plate.
Someone has ground coffee into the carpet.
The mill grinds corn for the whole county.

senses.head: Rub or scrape harshly
body: Of teeth and of gears — anything that grates under pressure. (скрежетать, тереть со скрипом)
examples: He grinds his teeth in his sleep.
The gears ground every time he shifted.

senses.head: Sharpen or shape on a wheel
body: Trade use: knives, lenses, valves. Do not confuse the past with the separate regular verb ground, grounded, meaning to keep a plane or a teenager at home. (точить, шлифовать)
examples: That shop grinds lenses to order.
They had ground the blade down to almost nothing.

senses.head: Grind to a halt
body: A fixed phrase for machinery or an effort stopping slowly and heavily. (постепенно остановиться, застопориться)
examples: Traffic had ground to a stop by seven.
The whole project ground to a halt in April.

senses.head: Grind down — wear someone out
body: Figurative, of pressure applied long enough to break resistance. (изматывать, изнурять)
examples: The commute grinds people down.
Six months of this has ground him down.

senses.head: Grind away, grind out
body: The source of the daily grind. Of dull, effortful, repetitive work. (корпеть; выдавать через силу)
examples: She grinds away at the same problem for weeks.
He has ground out four hundred pages of the thing.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary American, from grinding coffee to the daily grind
entries.contrast: The past ground is spelled and said exactly like the noun ground, the earth, and like a separate regular verb ground, grounded meaning to keep someone home or a plane out of the air: the flight was grounded, never ✗ the flight was ground.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a process verb of crushing and abrasion, and the source of the noun in the daily grind. Keep it apart from the separate regular verb ground, grounded (the flight was grounded, never ✗ the flight was ground).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the crushing, sharpening, and wearing-down senses (I grind the beans right before brewing, the commute grinds people down), intransitive in the grating and halting senses (the gears ground every time he shifted, traffic had ground to a stop).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the blade had been ground down to almost nothing, coffee has been ground into the carpet. No passive of traffic ground to a halt, and none of the homophonous grounded.
entries.phrasal verbs: grind away · grind down · grind on · grind out

entries.meaning: To fasten something so that it dangles, or to be suspended.
examples: We hang the wreath the day after Thanksgiving.
He hung his jacket on the back of the chair.
They have hung new blinds in every room.
A single bulb hangs over the table.
Smoke has hung over the valley for a week.
The portrait had hung in that hallway since 1962.
The state hanged him in 1892.
Three men had been hanged before the pardon arrived.
The deadline hangs over everything this week.
The lawsuit had hung over the family for years.
They hang out at the diner after practice.
We hung out until the place closed.
Hang on a second — I have the number here.
She hung on through two more rounds of layoffs.
He hung up on me.
Nobody has hung up a coat in this house in years.
The app hangs whenever I open that file.
The terminal had hung for ten minutes before I killed it.

senses.head: Suspend, put up
body: The transitive core sense, of pictures, coats, and laundry. (вешать, подвешивать)
examples: We hang the wreath the day after Thanksgiving.
He hung his jacket on the back of the chair.
They have hung new blinds in every room.

senses.head: Be suspended, dangle
body: The intransitive twin of sense 1. (висеть, свисать)
examples: A single bulb hangs over the table.
Smoke has hung over the valley for a week.
The portrait had hung in that hallway since 1962.

senses.head: Execute by hanging
body: This sense alone takes the regular hanged. Writing that a painting was hanged puts a rope around a canvas. (вешать (казнить))
examples: The state hanged him in 1892.
Three men had been hanged before the pardon arrived.

senses.head: Hang over — loom, threaten
body: Figurative, of debts, deadlines, and suspicion. (нависать, тяготеть над)
examples: The deadline hangs over everything this week.
The lawsuit had hung over the family for years.

senses.head: Hang out — spend time
body: Informal American, of relaxed, unplanned company. (тусоваться, зависать (разг.))
examples: They hang out at the diner after practice.
We hung out until the place closed.

senses.head: Hang on — wait; hold tight
body: Two senses of one phrasal: a spoken request to wait, and endurance under pressure. (подожди; держись)
examples: Hang on a second — I have the number here.
She hung on through two more rounds of layoffs.

senses.head: Hang up — end a call
body: From the days of a receiver on a hook, and still the ordinary word. (вешать трубку; повесить (на крючок))
examples: He hung up on me.
Nobody has hung up a coat in this house in years.

senses.head: Freeze, stop responding
body: Computing, intransitive. (зависать (о программе, компьютере))
examples: The app hangs whenever I open that file.
The terminal had hung for ten minutes before I killed it.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: The classic split in the language. Use hung for objects — I hung the picture — and the regular hanged only for execution: He was hanged at dawn. ✗ The painting was hanged puts a rope around a canvas.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic when you put something up (he hung his jacket); the intransitive twin is closer to a state of position (the portrait had hung in that hallway since 1962). The computing sense is eventive: the app hangs whenever I open that file.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the suspending, executing, and ending-a-call senses (we hang the wreath, the state hanged him in 1892), intransitive when something dangles, looms, freezes, or in the phrasals hang out and hang on (smoke has hung over the valley for a week).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — new blinds have been hung in every room. The execution sense keeps the regular form in the passive too: three men had been hanged before the pardon arrived, never ✗ three men had been hung. No passive of the intransitive a single bulb hangs over the table.
entries.phrasal verbs: hang around · hang back · hang in · hang on · hang on to · hang out · hang out with · hang over · hang together · hang up

entries.meaning: To lift or throw something heavy; of a ship, to move or come to rest.
examples: Two men heave the crates onto the dock every morning.
He heaved the box onto the truck.
They have heaved every sandbag on that pile.
Her shoulders heaved with every breath.
The sidewalk has heaved where the roots got under it.
She heaves a sigh every time the printer jams.
He heaved a sigh and signed it anyway.
The smell alone makes me heave.
He had heaved twice before we reached the dock.
The freighter hove into view just after dawn.
The schooner has hove to off the point.
By noon the whaler had hove alongside.

senses.head: Lift or throw something heavy
body: The everyday sense, and here American English is regular: heaved, heaved. (поднимать, швырять с усилием)
examples: Two men heave the crates onto the dock every morning.
He heaved the box onto the truck.
They have heaved every sandbag on that pile.

senses.head: Rise and fall heavily
