body: Of a chest after running, of a deck at sea, of ground buckling in a freeze. (тяжело вздыматься, ходить ходуном)
examples: Her shoulders heaved with every breath.
The sidewalk has heaved where the roots got under it.

senses.head: Heave a sigh
body: A fixed collocation; the object is nearly always a sigh. (тяжело вздохнуть)
examples: She heaves a sigh every time the printer jams.
He heaved a sigh and signed it anyway.

senses.head: Retch, vomit
body: Informal; the noun phrase is the dry heaves. (тошнить, рвать)
examples: The smell alone makes me heave.
He had heaved twice before we reached the dock.

senses.head: Move or come to rest (nautical)
body: This is the sense that carries hove, and it survives mainly in hove into view and hove to. (лечь в дрейф; показаться (о судне))
examples: The freighter hove into view just after dawn.
The schooner has hove to off the point.
By noon the whaler had hove alongside.

entries.register: neutral — ordinary in writing (heaved a sigh, heaved it onto the truck), less common in speech
entries.third person: heaves · -ing form: heaving (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: Everyday American English is regular: He heaved the box onto the truck. Hove is nautical, and it survives mainly in hove into view and hove to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; effortful motion, whether you supply the effort (he heaved the box onto the truck) or something else does (the sidewalk has heaved where the roots got under it).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the lifting sense and in the fixed heave a sigh (he heaved a sigh and signed it anyway), intransitive in the rising-and-falling, retching, and nautical senses (her shoulders heaved, the freighter hove into view).
entries.passive: restricted — the lifting sense passivizes (every sandbag on that pile has been heaved onto the dock), but the fixed collocation resists (✗ a sigh was heaved by her) and the nautical and retching senses are intransitive with no passive at all.

entries.meaning: To keep something in your hands, or to keep anything at all in a fixed state.
examples: Please hold the door.
He held the ladder while I climbed.
She has held that baby all afternoon.
That rope holds about three hundred pounds.
The shelf had held for years before it finally gave.
The tank holds forty gallons.
That room has held two hundred people before.
She had held the same job for nineteen years.
He holds two patents.
They have held a majority stake since 2019.
The board has held four meetings this quarter.
They held the election in November.
The court held that the statute did not apply.
Most economists hold the opposite view.
The rule holds in every case we tested.
That argument has held up remarkably well.
Police held him overnight.
They have held the shipment at customs since Monday.
Hold the onions on mine.
The hostess held our table for twenty minutes.
Hold your breath for five seconds.
He held the note longer than anyone thought he could.
Hold on — I have the number right here.
The roof held out through the whole storm.
She has held off on buying anything until spring.

senses.head: Grasp, keep in the hands
body: The literal core sense. There is no form holded, and every compound follows suit. (держать (в руках))
examples: Please hold the door.
He held the ladder while I climbed.
She has held that baby all afternoon.

senses.head: Bear weight, stay fastened
body: Intransitive, of anything under load. Watch the near-twin hole up, to hide away, whose past holed sounds exactly like hold. (выдерживать, держаться)
examples: That rope holds about three hundred pounds.
The shelf had held for years before it finally gave.

senses.head: Contain, have room for
body: Capacity, of tanks, rooms, and containers. (вмещать, содержать)
examples: The tank holds forty gallons.
That room has held two hundred people before.

senses.head: Occupy or own
body: Of a job, a title, a degree, a record, or a stake in something. (занимать (должность); владеть (акциями, титулом))
examples: She had held the same job for nineteen years.
He holds two patents.
They have held a majority stake since 2019.

senses.head: Conduct, stage an event
body: Meetings, elections, hearings, funerals. (проводить (собрание, выборы))
examples: The board has held four meetings this quarter.
They held the election in November.

senses.head: Believe, maintain, rule
body: Formal, usually hold that. In legal writing a court holds something, and the ruling itself is a holding. (придерживаться мнения; постановить)
examples: The court held that the statute did not apply.
Most economists hold the opposite view.

senses.head: Remain true or valid
body: Intransitive, of rules, theories, and arguments: the rule holds, that holds true. (оставаться в силе, быть верным)
examples: The rule holds in every case we tested.
That argument has held up remarkably well.

senses.head: Detain, keep in custody
body: Of police, hospitals, and customs. (задерживать, держать под стражей)
examples: Police held him overnight.
They have held the shipment at customs since Monday.

senses.head: Keep back, reserve
body: To withhold or set aside — including the diner sense: hold the onions. (придержать; не класть (в заказе))
examples: Hold the onions on mine.
The hostess held our table for twenty minutes.

senses.head: Hold a breath, a note
body: To sustain something that naturally wants to stop. (задерживать (дыхание), выдерживать (ноту))
examples: Hold your breath for five seconds.
He held the note longer than anyone thought he could.

senses.head: Hold on, hold off, hold out
body: Three common phrasals: hold on means wait, hold off means delay, and hold out means last or refuse to give in. (подождать; повременить; продержаться)
examples: Hold on — I have the number right here.
The roof held out through the whole storm.
She has held off on buying anything until spring.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Held is the only past; ✗ holded never appears, and every compound follows suit — behold, uphold, withhold. Watch the near-twin hole up, meaning to hide away: it is a regular verb, and its past holed /hoʊld/ sounds exactly like hold. We holed up in a cabin is the hiding; ✗ we held up in a cabin says they robbed it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the grasping, staging, and detaining senses (they held the election in November); stative in the capacity, possession, and belief senses, which resist the progressive: ✗ the tank is holding forty gallons, ✗ he is holding two patents, ✗ most economists are holding the opposite view.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in most senses (he held the ladder, police held him overnight, hold your breath), intransitive in the load-bearing and validity senses (that rope holds about three hundred pounds, the rule holds in every case we tested).
entries.passive: restricted — the dynamic senses go freely (the election was held in November, the shipment has been held at customs), and so does the occupying sense in formal registers (a majority stake is held by the family). But the containing sense refuses outright: ✗ forty gallons are held by the tank, ✗ two hundred people have been held by that room.
entries.phrasal verbs: hold against · hold back · hold down · hold forth · hold off · hold on · hold on to · hold out · hold out for · hold out on · hold over · hold together · hold up · hold with

entries.meaning: To breed with a different variety, population, or species.
examples: The two populations interbreed wherever their ranges overlap.
Wolves and coyotes interbred along the Great Lakes.
Biologists say the subspecies have interbred for millennia.
Breeders interbreed the lines to fix the coat color.
The station has interbred wheat varieties since the 1930s.
That flock interbreeds with the wild birds every spring.
The valley families had interbred so long that everyone shared a surname.

senses.head: Breed across populations
body: Intransitive, and the ordinary biological sense. (скрещиваться (о видах, породах))
examples: The two populations interbreed wherever their ranges overlap.
Wolves and coyotes interbred along the Great Lakes.
Biologists say the subspecies have interbred for millennia.

senses.head: Cause two lines to breed together
body: Transitive, with a breeder or a research station as the subject. (скрещивать (породы, линии))
examples: Breeders interbreed the lines to fix the coat color.
The station has interbred wheat varieties since the 1930s.

senses.head: Marry within a closed group
body: Of people, and usually with a suggestion of too small a gene pool. (заключать браки внутри своей группы)
examples: That flock interbreeds with the wild birds every spring.
The valley families had interbred so long that everyone shared a surname.

entries.register: rare — a biologist's word; ordinary speech says mix or cross
entries.contrast: It follows breed.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, eventive when populations mix on their own and causative when a breeder or a station drives it.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in the ordinary biological sense (the two populations interbreed wherever their ranges overlap, the valley families had interbred for generations), transitive when someone causes it (breeders interbreed the lines to fix the coat color).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — wheat varieties have been interbred since the 1930s, the lines are interbred to fix the coat color. No passive of the intransitive wolves and coyotes interbred.

entries.meaning: To go in front and show the way, or to be in charge of something.
examples: The ranger led us up the switchbacks.
She leads the group out at seven sharp.
He has led three expeditions to that range.
She leads the Tuesday standup.
He led the department for six years.
She has led the team since the merger.
This trail should lead you straight to the falls.
The clues had led us to the wrong house entirely.
That decision has led to a lot of confusion.
One question led to another.
They lead the division by four games.
She led from the first lap to the last.
They lead a quiet life out there.
He has led an unusually complicated life.
He led her on for months.
Nobody has led you on about the timeline.
Every paper led with the same photo.
She led off the meeting with the budget.

senses.head: Guide, go in front of
body: The literal sense. The commonest spelling error in American writing is putting lead where the past led belongs — the metal lead is pronounced the same and tempts the fingers. (вести, идти впереди)
examples: The ranger led us up the switchbacks.
She leads the group out at seven sharp.
He has led three expeditions to that range.

senses.head: Direct, be in charge of
body: Of teams, departments, and organizations. (руководить, возглавлять)
examples: She leads the Tuesday standup.
He led the department for six years.
She has led the team since the merger.

senses.head: Lead somewhere (of a road)
body: Intransitive, with an inanimate subject. (вести (о дороге, двери))
examples: This trail should lead you straight to the falls.
The clues had led us to the wrong house entirely.

senses.head: Lead to — result in
body: Causation, and one of the most common verb phrases in expository writing. (приводить к, вести к)
examples: That decision has led to a lot of confusion.
One question led to another.

senses.head: Be ahead, be in front
body: Sports and polling: lead by four, lead the division. (лидировать, вести в счёте)
examples: They lead the division by four games.
She led from the first lap to the last.

senses.head: Lead a life
body: A fixed collocation; the object is always a life or an existence. (вести (образ жизни))
examples: They lead a quiet life out there.
He has led an unusually complicated life.

senses.head: Lead someone on
body: To encourage a hope, usually a romantic one, that you do not intend to satisfy. (водить за нос, обнадёживать напрасно)
examples: He led her on for months.
Nobody has led you on about the timeline.

senses.head: Lead with, lead off
body: Journalism and meetings: to open with a particular item. (начинать с (чего-л.))
examples: Every paper led with the same photo.
She led off the meeting with the budget.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: The single commonest spelling error in American writing. The metal lead is pronounced /lɛd/, exactly like the past tense led, and the sound tempts people into ✗ He lead the team last year. The past of this verb is always spelled led.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; guiding literally (the ranger led us up the switchbacks), directing an organization (she leads the team), and causing in lead to (one question led to another).
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a person, a group, or a life as object (he led the department for six years, they lead a quiet life), intransitive in the road, scoring, and lead to senses (this trail should lead you straight to the falls, they lead the division by four games).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the department was led by her for six years, he was led on for months, we were led to the wrong house entirely. No passive of lead to: ✗ a lot of confusion has been led to.
entries.phrasal verbs: lead off · lead on · lead to · lead up to

entries.meaning: To set something burning, or to fill a place with light.
examples: We light the fireplace on the first cold night.
He lit the grill with a long match.
Someone has lit every candle on the table.
That one lamp lights the whole room.
The crew had lit the runway before the plane turned in.
Her whole face lights up when he calls.
The board lit up with warnings.
He lit a cigarette on the porch.
She has lit up twice since we sat down.
Her eye lit on the one line that mattered.
A moth had lit on the screen door.
They lit out for California the next morning.
He had lit out before anyone noticed he was gone.

senses.head: Set burning, ignite
body: Candles, grills, fires, fuses. Both lit and lighted are standard American English, but lit is the usual past. (зажигать, поджигать)
examples: We light the fireplace on the first cold night.
He lit the grill with a long match.
Someone has lit every candle on the table.

senses.head: Illuminate, give light to
body: Of lamps and windows. Lighted is most at home in front of a noun: a lighted window. (освещать)
examples: That one lamp lights the whole room.
The crew had lit the runway before the plane turned in.

senses.head: Light up — brighten
body: Of a face with pleasure, or a panel with signals. (озаряться, загораться (о лице, экране))
examples: Her whole face lights up when he calls.
The board lit up with warnings.

senses.head: Light a cigarette; light up
body: Informal, and usually with no object at all: he lit up on the porch. (закурить)
examples: He lit a cigarette on the porch.
She has lit up twice since we sat down.

senses.head: Light on, light upon
body: To come to rest on something, literally or with the eye. Overlaps with the separate verb alight. (останавливаться (взглядом); натыкаться на)
examples: Her eye lit on the one line that mattered.
A moth had lit on the screen door.

senses.head: Light out — leave fast
body: Dated American slang, famous from the last line of Huckleberry Finn. (смыться, дать дёру)
examples: They lit out for California the next morning.
He had lit out before anyone noticed he was gone.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Both lit and lighted are standard American English. Lit is the usual past and participle — she lit the candles — while lighted is most at home in front of a noun: a lighted match, a lighted window.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic. The participle lighted doubles as an adjective in front of a noun (a lighted match, a lighted window), where lit is less at home.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the igniting and illuminating senses (he lit the grill with a long match, that one lamp lights the whole room), intransitive in light up, light on, and the dated slang light out (her whole face lights up when he calls, a moth had lit on the screen door).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — every candle on the table has been lit, the runway had been lit before the plane turned in. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ California was lit out for.
entries.phrasal verbs: light on · light out · light up

entries.meaning: To come together with someone, or to satisfy a requirement.
examples: I met her standing in line at the DMV.
We meet every other Thursday.
They have met twice since the merger.
Meet my brother Danny.
We met at a wedding in 2011.
The committee meets on the first Monday of the month.
The board has met four times this year.
This proposal meets all three conditions.
He had met the deadline by about four minutes.
Can you meet my flight on Sunday?
She met us at baggage claim.
The two trails meet just above the falls.
The seams had met unevenly along the whole hem.
The plan met fierce resistance.
The proposal has met with a lot of skepticism.
He would not meet my eye all evening.
They met us halfway on the price.

senses.head: Encounter, come together with
body: The core sense, whether arranged or by chance. (встречать, встречаться)
examples: I met her standing in line at the DMV.
We meet every other Thursday.
They have met twice since the merger.

senses.head: Be introduced to
body: First contact only. Once you have met someone, you see them from then on. (знакомиться)
examples: Meet my brother Danny.
We met at a wedding in 2011.

senses.head: Assemble, convene
body: Of a committee, a board, or a class, with the group as subject. (собираться, заседать)
examples: The committee meets on the first Monday of the month.
The board has met four times this year.

senses.head: Satisfy a requirement
body: The object is a standard, a deadline, a need, or a quota. (соответствовать, отвечать (требованиям))
examples: This proposal meets all three conditions.
He had met the deadline by about four minutes.

senses.head: Go to receive an arrival
body: You meet a flight or meet someone at the airport by being there when they land. (встречать (на вокзале, в аэропорту))
examples: Can you meet my flight on Sunday?
She met us at baggage claim.

senses.head: Join, come into contact
body: Of roads, rivers, edges, and lines, with inanimate subjects. (сходиться, соединяться)
examples: The two trails meet just above the falls.
The seams had met unevenly along the whole hem.

senses.head: Face, encounter (resistance, a fate)
body: Often meet with: met with resistance, met his death. (столкнуться с; встретить (конец, сопротивление))
examples: The plan met fierce resistance.
The proposal has met with a lot of skepticism.

senses.head: Meet someone's eye; meet halfway
body: Two fixed phrases — refusing eye contact, and compromising. (встретиться взглядом; пойти навстречу)
examples: He would not meet my eye all evening.
They met us halfway on the price.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Met is the only past, and ✗ meeted is never right. Three words crowd the sound /mit/: this verb, the meat you eat, and mete, to hand out. Mete is regular, so a judge meted out a sentence — never ✗ met out.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the encountering, convening, and receiving senses; closer to stative in the requirement sense, which states a fact rather than an event: ✗ this proposal is meeting all three conditions.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a person, a standard, or an arrival as object (I met her standing in line at the DMV, this proposal meets all three conditions, she met us at baggage claim), intransitive when the parties are the joint subject (we meet every other Thursday, the two trails meet just above the falls).
entries.passive: restricted — the requirement sense passivizes best of all: all three conditions are met, the deadline was met by about four minutes, and so does the receiving sense: we were met at baggage claim. The plain encountering sense resists: ✗ she was met by me standing in line at the DMV.
entries.phrasal verbs: meet up · meet up with · meet with

entries.meaning: To give someone a false impression, on purpose or by accident.
examples: He misleads people without ever quite lying.
The label misled thousands of buyers.
Nobody has misled you about the price.
These charts mislead more than they explain.
The brochure had misled us about the distance to the beach.
Bad company had misled him early.
She swore that nobody misled her into signing it.

senses.head: Deceive deliberately
body: Deception that avoids an outright lie. The past is misled, said mis-LED — never spelled mislead. (вводить в заблуждение, обманывать)
examples: He misleads people without ever quite lying.
The label misled thousands of buyers.
Nobody has misled you about the price.

senses.head: Create a false impression unintentionally
body: Of charts, statistics, names, and signs. The adjective misleading is commoner than the verb here. (сбивать с толку, вводить в заблуждение (невольно))
examples: These charts mislead more than they explain.
The brochure had misled us about the distance to the beach.

senses.head: Lead astray
body: Older and moralizing: to draw someone into bad conduct. (сбивать с пути, совращать)
examples: Bad company had misled him early.
She swore that nobody misled her into signing it.

entries.register: everyday — common in speech and writing alike, above all as misleading
entries.contrast: It follows lead, spelling trap and all: the past is misled, never ✗ mislead. And misled is said /ˌmɪsˈlɛd/ — mis-LED. Readers who take it for a single word famously mispronounce it MY-zuld.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and causative: it produces a false impression, deliberately or not. The participle misleading has become an ordinary adjective, commoner than the verb itself.
entries.transitivity: transitive, with the deceived person as object (the label misled thousands of buyers); the object may be dropped when the general effect is the point (these charts mislead more than they explain).
entries.passive: yes — thousands of buyers were misled by the label, we had been misled about the distance to the beach, nobody has been misled about the price.

entries.meaning: To take someone's meaning wrongly.
examples: I misunderstood the invitation and showed up a day early.
People regularly misunderstand that policy.
She has misunderstood my email twice now.
Half the class misunderstood the assignment.
They had misunderstood the terms before they ever signed.
He misunderstands every joke and laughs anyway.
Critics have misunderstood her work from the start.
He was a misunderstood kid who turned out fine.

senses.head: Take a meaning wrongly
body: The core sense, of words, instructions, and intentions. (неправильно понять)
examples: I misunderstood the invitation and showed up a day early.
People regularly misunderstand that policy.
She has misunderstood my email twice now.

senses.head: Fail to grasp a subject
body: Of a task, a rule, or a body of material rather than a single remark. (не разобраться, неверно понять (предмет, условия))
examples: Half the class misunderstood the assignment.
They had misunderstood the terms before they ever signed.

senses.head: Misjudge a person
body: Often passive and sympathetic: a misunderstood artist, a misunderstood kid. (неверно судить о ком-л.)
examples: He misunderstands every joke and laughs anyway.
Critics have misunderstood her work from the start.
He was a misunderstood kid who turned out fine.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary American; you misunderstood me is plain conversation
entries.contrast: It follows understand, which follows stand.
entries.verb type: stative — like understand, it names a state of comprehension rather than an activity, so the progressive is limited to the ongoing-error reading (I think I'm misunderstanding you); ✗ she is misunderstanding my email twice is not available.
entries.transitivity: transitive, with the words, the material, or the person misread as object (half the class misunderstood the assignment, critics have misunderstood her work from the start); the object is dropped only when context supplies it (sorry, I misunderstood).
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is very common — her work has been misunderstood from the start, the terms had been misunderstood before anyone signed. The participle is also a plain adjective: a misunderstood kid.

entries.meaning: To defeat someone in combat, or simply to fight better than they do.
examples: Smaller crews sometimes outfight bigger ones.
He outfought a taller opponent for twelve rounds.
That regiment has outfought every unit it has faced.
She outfights everyone in her weight class without ever knocking anyone out.
The champion outfought him on the inside for eight rounds.
Underdogs had outfought the favorites for most of the tournament.

senses.head: Beat in a fight
body: The core sense: to win a physical fight, or to prevail over a stronger enemy in war. It follows fight exactly, so the past and participle are both outfought. (побеждать в бою, одолевать)
examples: Smaller crews sometimes outfight bigger ones.
He outfought a taller opponent for twelve rounds.
That regiment has outfought every unit it has faced.

senses.head: Outwork an opponent (boxing, MMA)
body: Ring commentary: to land the better and busier work over a bout without necessarily finishing anyone. Extends to any contest won by effort rather than by a decisive blow. (переигрывать, превосходить по технике)
examples: She outfights everyone in her weight class without ever knocking anyone out.
The champion outfought him on the inside for eight rounds.
Underdogs had outfought the favorites for most of the tournament.

entries.register: rare — a prefixed derivative recognized but seldom produced, and mostly by sportswriters
entries.contrast: It follows fight.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; a comparative verb built on fight, meaning to fight better than the other side, mostly in sportswriting.
entries.transitivity: transitive, with the opponent as an obligatory object — he outfought a taller opponent for twelve rounds; ✗ smaller crews sometimes outfight is incomplete.
entries.passive: yes, though the active is far commoner — the favorites had been outfought for most of the tournament, he was outfought on the inside for eight rounds.

entries.meaning: To be much more impressive than someone or something else, or literally to give off more light.
examples: A good opening line can outshine a whole chapter.
The understudy outshone the lead.
That one dessert has outshone everything else on the menu.
A full moon outshines every star in the sky.
The stadium lights outshone the fireworks.
Venus had outshone everything else on the horizon by dusk.

senses.head: Be far more impressive than
body: The everyday sense, and the one you will meet in reviews and in office talk. (затмевать, превосходить)
examples: A good opening line can outshine a whole chapter.
The understudy outshone the lead.
That one dessert has outshone everything else on the menu.

senses.head: Give off more light than
body: The literal sense, less common than the figurative one. Only outshone in edited prose; outshined turns up in speech and in song lyrics. (светить ярче)
examples: A full moon outshines every star in the sky.
The stadium lights outshone the fireworks.
Venus had outshone everything else on the horizon by dusk.

entries.register: neutral — ordinary in reviews and profiles, less common in casual speech
entries.third person: outshines · -ing form: outshining (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: It follows shine, but only the shone branch: since it never means to polish, it keeps outshone. Outshined turns up in speech and in song lyrics, not in edited prose.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, the figurative outshine the lead and the literal outshine every star; no linking or stative use
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is obligatory, since you always outshine someone or something: ✗ the understudy outshone is incomplete
entries.passive: yes — the lead was outshone by the understudy, everything else on the menu has been outshone by that one dessert

entries.meaning: To give too much food to a person or animal, or too much of anything to a system that cannot absorb it.
examples: New owners almost always overfeed their fish.
We overfed the dog over the holidays.
He has overfed every guest who ever sat at that table.
Don't overfeed the lawn with nitrogen.
A stuck float overfed the carburetor and the engine flooded.
Cheap credit had overfed the housing market for years.

senses.head: Give too much food
body: The literal sense, used of pets, fish, livestock, and guests. (перекармливать)
examples: New owners almost always overfeed their fish.
We overfed the dog over the holidays.
He has overfed every guest who ever sat at that table.

senses.head: Oversupply a system
body: Extended to fertilizer, fuel, data, or money — anything supplied faster than it can be used. Before a noun the participle pulls its stress forward: an overfed market. (перенасыщать, давать сверх меры)
examples: Don't overfeed the lawn with nitrogen.
A stuck float overfed the carburetor and the engine flooded.
Cheap credit had overfed the housing market for years.

entries.register: neutral — plain but narrow; mostly advice about pets, fish, and babies
entries.contrast: It follows feed. Used in front of a noun, the participle pulls its stress to the front: an overfed cat /ˈoʊvərˌfɛd/.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, of feeding animals and of oversupplying a system (cheap credit overfed the housing market)
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is obligatory: ✗ new owners overfeed is incomplete without their fish
entries.passive: yes — the fish are overfed by almost every new owner, the carburetor was overfed by a stuck float. The participle also works attributively: an overfed cat.

entries.meaning: To stick out over something below, or, figuratively, to loom over it.
examples: Those branches overhang the driveway.
A dead limb overhung the porch all summer.
The cliff has overhung that trail since the last slide.
Layoffs overhang every conversation in that building.
Debt has overhung the company since the buyout.
The lawsuit had overhung the merger for two years.

senses.head: Project out over
body: Physical: a roof, a branch, or a cliff extending past whatever is under it. It follows hang on the hung branch only, since there is no execution sense, so ✗ overhanged never appears. (нависать, выступать над)
examples: Those branches overhang the driveway.
A dead limb overhung the porch all summer.
The cliff has overhung that trail since the last slide.

senses.head: Loom over, weigh on
body: Figurative, usually of debt, suspicion, or a threat that has not yet come to anything. Very common in business writing. (тяготеть над, довлеть)
examples: Layoffs overhang every conversation in that building.
Debt has overhung the company since the buyout.
The lawsuit had overhung the merger for two years.

entries.register: rare — architectural and geological; the noun an overhang is far commoner than the verb
entries.contrast: It follows hang, but only the hung branch — there is no execution sense, so ✗ overhanged never appears. The noun overhang moves the stress to the front: /ˈoʊvərˌhæŋ/.
entries.verb type: stative in the positional sense — those branches overhang the driveway reports where something is, not something done; the figurative debt overhangs the company is stative too
entries.transitivity: transitive — what is overhung is named: overhang the driveway, overhang every conversation
entries.passive: restricted — the descriptive passive is fine (a trail overhung by a dead limb, the porch was overhung with vines), but because the verb is stative there is no event to passivize: ✗ the driveway was overhung by the branches yesterday reads oddly

entries.meaning: To go past the point you were aiming for, in space or in measure.
examples: Pilots overshoot that runway in a crosswind.
We overshot the exit by four miles.
She has overshot the driveway twice this week.
Big projects always overshoot their budgets.
Costs overshot the estimate by a third.
Inflation had overshot the target for six straight quarters.
If you overshoot, go around and try again.
The 737 overshot the runway in the rain.
Two aircraft had overshot before the tower closed the field.

senses.head: Go past the target point
body: The literal sense, of drivers, runners, and anything else that travels too far. (проскочить, промахнуться мимо цели)
examples: Pilots overshoot that runway in a crosswind.
We overshot the exit by four miles.
She has overshot the driveway twice this week.

senses.head: Exceed a limit or estimate
body: Of budgets, deadlines, inflation, and growth — anything that runs past a planned figure. Standard in business and economics writing. (превысить (норму, смету))
examples: Big projects always overshoot their budgets.
Costs overshot the estimate by a third.
Inflation had overshot the target for six straight quarters.

senses.head: Land long, aviation
body: Technical: to touch down too far along the runway, or to fail to land within it at all. The noun and adjective take front stress — an overshot landing, an overshot jaw. (проскочить полосу, уйти на второй круг)
examples: If you overshoot, go around and try again.
The 737 overshot the runway in the rain.
Two aircraft had overshot before the tower closed the field.

entries.register: neutral — ordinary in aviation, economics, and journalism; less common in speech
entries.contrast: It follows shoot. As a noun or an adjective the word shifts its stress to the front: an overshot jaw /ˈoʊvərˌʃɑt/.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: passing a point (we overshot the exit), exceeding a figure (costs overshot the estimate), and landing long
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the ordinary uses (overshoot the runway, overshoot their budgets), intransitive in aviation (if you overshoot, go around)
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the runway was overshot in the rain, the target had been overshot for six straight quarters. No passive of the intransitive if you overshoot.

entries.meaning: To answer a criminal charge in court, or to beg someone earnestly.
examples: Defendants plead not guilty at arraignment.
He pled guilty to a lesser charge.
She has pled not guilty to all four counts.
Don't plead with him; he decided a week ago.
She pled with the landlord twice this month.
They had pled for more time before the judge cut them off.
She pleads every case the same way.
The firm pled the matter in federal court.
Counsel has pled this issue three times already.
You cannot just plead ignorance and walk away.
He pled the Fifth rather than answer.
She had pled exhaustion and gone home early.

senses.head: Enter a plea in court
body: Fixed with guilty, not guilty, or no contest, and with no preposition: you plead guilty, never ✗ plead to be guilty. Both pled and pleaded are standard American pasts here. (заявлять о признании вины (в суде))
examples: Defendants plead not guilty at arraignment.
He pled guilty to a lesser charge.
She has pled not guilty to all four counts.

senses.head: Beg, appeal earnestly
body: Takes with before the person and for before the thing: plead with your boss for more time. (умолять, упрашивать)
examples: Don't plead with him; he decided a week ago.
She pled with the landlord twice this month.
They had pled for more time before the judge cut them off.

senses.head: Argue a case as an attorney
body: Formal legal use, and the source of the noun pleadings. (выступать в суде, вести дело)
examples: She pleads every case the same way.
The firm pled the matter in federal court.
Counsel has pled this issue three times already.

senses.head: Offer as an excuse or defense
body: Fixed objects: plead ignorance, plead poverty, plead insanity, plead the Fifth. What is pleaded is the reason you give, not something you necessarily believe. (ссылаться на (что-л. в оправдание))
examples: You cannot just plead ignorance and walk away.
He pled the Fifth rather than answer.
She had pled exhaustion and gone home early.

entries.register: everyday — the courtroom sense is in every news report, and plead with is ordinary speech
entries.contrast: Both forms are standard American English. Pleaded is the older one and the choice of most newspaper style guides — she pleaded guilty — while pled is very common in speech and around courthouses. Neither is an error.
entries.verb type: action — a speech-act verb, dynamic in every sense: entering a plea, begging, arguing a case, offering an excuse
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with a preposition when it means beg (plead with him, plead for more time), transitive with a fixed complement elsewhere (plead guilty, plead the Fifth, plead the matter in federal court); note ✗ plead to be guilty
entries.passive: restricted — natural where a case or a defense is the object (the issue has been pled three times, insanity was pleaded), but the fixed complements resist: ✗ not guilty was pled by him, and the plead with sense is intransitive and has no passive at all

entries.meaning: To film or photograph something over again.
examples: We reshoot anything the client flags.
He reshoots every portrait he isn't sure about.
The studio reshot the ending twice.
They have reshot half the movie.
The crew had reshot the scene before lunch.

senses.head: Film or photograph again
body: Used of movie scenes and of still photography alike, and it follows shoot in every form. The noun a reshoot takes front stress: /ˈriˌʃut/. (переснимать, снимать заново)
examples: We reshoot anything the client flags.
He reshoots every portrait he isn't sure about.
The studio reshot the ending twice.
They have reshot half the movie.
The crew had reshot the scene before lunch.

entries.register: rare — film and photography jargon; the noun is commoner than the past tense
entries.contrast: It follows shoot. The noun a reshoot takes front stress: /ˈriˌʃut/.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a straightforward repetition verb built on shoot
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is normally obligatory (reshoot the ending), though it can go unexpressed when the scene is understood: we reshoot anything the client flags
entries.passive: yes — the ending was reshot twice, half the movie has been reshot

entries.meaning: To wind something back toward the beginning, literally or figuratively.
examples: Rewind it about ten seconds.
He rewound the tape and played it again.
I have rewound this song four times.
Let's rewind to the part where you agreed to pay.
She rewound the whole argument on the drive home.
He has rewound that conversation a hundred times.
A good shop can rewind that motor for less than a new one costs.
They rewound the armature by hand.
The generator had been rewound twice before it failed for good.

senses.head: Wind tape or film back
body: The original sense, from cassettes and reels; it survives on every video player and podcast app. (перематывать назад)
examples: Rewind it about ten seconds.
He rewound the tape and played it again.
I have rewound this song four times.

senses.head: Go back over something
body: Figurative, borrowed from the tape sense: to replay a moment in your head, or to restart a conversation. Often an interjection — rewind, say that again. (отмотать назад, вернуться к началу)
examples: Let's rewind to the part where you agreed to pay.
She rewound the whole argument on the drive home.
He has rewound that conversation a hundred times.

senses.head: Rewire a motor or coil
body: Technical, in electrical and machine-shop work: to replace the winding on a motor, a transformer, or a generator. (перематывать обмотку)
examples: A good shop can rewind that motor for less than a new one costs.
They rewound the armature by hand.
The generator had been rewound twice before it failed for good.

entries.register: everyday — still ordinary for video and, figuratively, for going back over something
entries.contrast: It follows wind /waɪnd/, so the base rhymes with find, not with the noun wind that blows.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: winding tape back, replaying a moment in your head, or rewinding a motor coil
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a tape, a conversation, or an armature (he rewound the tape), intransitive in the figurative let's rewind to the part where you agreed to pay and the interjection rewind, say that again
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the armature was rewound by hand, the generator had been rewound twice

entries.meaning: To give off or reflect light, or to be conspicuously good at something.
examples: The porch light shines all night.
The sun shone through the whole ceremony.
That lamp has shone since Tuesday without a break.
Her hair shines in that light.
The wet street shone under the headlights.
The old table has shone like new since we oiled it.
New quarterbacks rarely shine in their first start.
She shone in the second act.
He has shone in every crisis this company has had.
Shine the light over here.
He shined his phone into the crawlspace.
The deputy has shined a spotlight on every car that passes.
He shines his own shoes every Sunday.
She shined the silver before the guests came.
Somebody has shined every trophy in that case.
Her patience shines through even on the worst days.
His nerves shone through in the first ten minutes.
The original color has shone through where the paint wore thin.

senses.head: Give off light
body: The core intransitive sense, and the one that takes shone. Americans say /ʃoʊn/, rhyming with bone; the British say /ʃɒn/, rhyming with gone. (светить, сиять)
examples: The porch light shines all night.
The sun shone through the whole ceremony.
That lamp has shone since Tuesday without a break.

senses.head: Gleam, look glossy
body: Of a surface that reflects rather than emits — hair, wet pavement, polished wood. (блестеть, лосниться)
examples: Her hair shines in that light.
The wet street shone under the headlights.
The old table has shone like new since we oiled it.

senses.head: Excel, stand out
body: Figurative: to be visibly better than everyone around you, especially in a moment that puts it on display. (блистать, отличаться)
examples: New quarterbacks rarely shine in their first start.
She shone in the second act.
He has shone in every crisis this company has had.

senses.head: Aim a light at something
body: Transitive, and here the past is the regular shined: she shined the flashlight at us. ✗ She shone the flashlight is not standard American English. (направлять свет, светить (чем-л.))
examples: Shine the light over here.
He shined his phone into the crawlspace.
The deputy has shined a spotlight on every car that passes.

senses.head: Polish
body: Always the regular shined — shined shoes, never ✗ shone shoes. (начищать, наводить блеск)
examples: He shines his own shoes every Sunday.
She shined the silver before the guests came.
Somebody has shined every trophy in that case.

senses.head: shine through
body: Of a quality that shows itself despite everything laid over it. (проступать, проявляться)
examples: Her patience shines through even on the worst days.
His nerves shone through in the first ten minutes.
The original color has shone through where the paint wore thin.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.third person: shines · -ing form: shining (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: Two things to watch. Meaning splits the forms: shone when the verb means gave off light — the sun shone all week — and the regular shined when it means polished, he shined his shoes, or when the verb takes an object, she shined the flashlight at us. The vowel splits by country: Americans say shone /ʃoʊn/, rhyming with bone; the British say /ʃɒn/, rhyming with gone.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, though the light senses are close to a continuous state (the porch light shines all night); no linking use
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive when it means give off light, gleam, or excel (the sun shone, she shone in the second act), transitive when it means aim a light or polish (he shined his phone into the crawlspace, she shined the silver)
entries.passive: restricted — yes in the transitive senses, and there the past is the regular shined: his shoes are shined every Sunday, a spotlight has been shined on every car. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ all week was shone by the sun.
entries.phrasal verbs: shine through

entries.meaning: To fire a weapon, to send something moving fast, or to record images with a camera.
examples: They shoot skeet out past the tree line.
Someone shot out the streetlight again.
He has shot competitively since high school.
They shoot the commercial in Utah.
She shoots film, not digital.
The director had shot the whole scene before the rain came.
Shoot from the corner if he leaves you open.
He shot the free throw with two seconds left.
She has shot forty percent from three all season.
Kids shoot out of that school at three o'clock.
Pain shot up my arm.
A cat had shot across the road before I could brake.
Prices shoot up every summer.
Rent shot up forty percent in two years.
He has shot up four inches since Christmas.
Anti-aircraft crews shoot down what they can see.
The committee shot down the proposal in ten minutes.
She has shot down every plan we have brought her.
Let's shoot for Friday.
They shot for a spring release and missed it.
We have shot for that number three quarters in a row.
Shoot me an email when you land.
I shot him a text from the parking lot.
She has shot me three links already.
Bamboo shoots up as soon as the ground warms.
The vines shot six feet in a single season.
The seed potatoes have shot in the bag.

senses.head: Fire a weapon; hit with a bullet
body: The core sense, transitive or intransitive. Shot is the only past — ✗ shooted never appears — and it doubles as an adjective: shot nerves, the clutch is shot. (стрелять; застрелить)
examples: They shoot skeet out past the tree line.
Someone shot out the streetlight again.
He has shot competitively since high school.

senses.head: Film or photograph
body: The standard verb in film and photography: shoot a movie, a scene, a wedding, a roll of film. (снимать (фильм, фото))
examples: They shoot the commercial in Utah.
She shoots film, not digital.
The director had shot the whole scene before the rain came.

senses.head: Take a shot at a goal or basket
body: Sports. Also used of the score a golfer posts — he shot a 68 — and of shooting percentages. (бить (по воротам), бросать (по кольцу))
examples: Shoot from the corner if he leaves you open.
He shot the free throw with two seconds left.
She has shot forty percent from three all season.

senses.head: Move fast, dart
body: Intransitive, of anything that moves suddenly and quickly — a car, a person, a pain running up an arm. (промчаться, метнуться)
examples: Kids shoot out of that school at three o'clock.
Pain shot up my arm.
A cat had shot across the road before I could brake.

senses.head: shoot up — rise sharply
body: Of prices, temperature, or a growing child. A separate slang sense of shoot up, meaning to inject a drug, is also common and always clear from context. (резко подскочить, взлететь)
examples: Prices shoot up every summer.
Rent shot up forty percent in two years.
He has shot up four inches since Christmas.

senses.head: shoot down
body: Literally of an aircraft, figuratively of a proposal or a suggestion. (сбить (самолёт); отвергнуть (идею))
examples: Anti-aircraft crews shoot down what they can see.
The committee shot down the proposal in ten minutes.
She has shot down every plan we have brought her.

senses.head: shoot for — aim at
body: Informal, of a target date or a goal: we're shooting for Friday. (стремиться к, метить на)
examples: Let's shoot for Friday.
They shot for a spring release and missed it.
We have shot for that number three quarters in a row.

senses.head: Send quickly
body: Informal but very common in American workplaces, with a double object: shoot me an email, shoot her a text. (быстро отправить, скинуть)
examples: Shoot me an email when you land.
I shot him a text from the parking lot.
She has shot me three links already.

senses.head: Put out shoots, of a plant
body: Intransitive and horticultural — the source of the noun a shoot, a new green stem. (давать побеги, прорастать)
examples: Bamboo shoots up as soon as the ground warms.
The vines shot six feet in a single season.
The seed potatoes have shot in the bag.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Shot is the only past; ✗ shooted never appears. The word doubles as a noun (a good shot) and an adjective (shot nerves, the clutch is shot). The base is a homophone of chute, the slide or the parachute, which has no verb forms of its own.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from firing a weapon to filming to a plant putting out shoots
entries.transitivity: both, and ditransitive in one informal sense — intransitive in pain shot up my arm and the vines shot six feet, transitive in someone shot out the streetlight and they shoot the commercial in Utah, ditransitive in shoot me an email
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — he was shot in the arm, the whole scene had been shot before the rain came, the proposal was shot down in ten minutes. The ditransitive resists: ✗ I was shot an email is not idiomatic; and the intransitive kids shoot out of that school has no passive.
entries.phrasal verbs: shoot down · shoot for · shoot up

entries.meaning: To rest on your seat, to be positioned somewhere, or to serve as a member of a body.
examples: We sit in the back row.
He sat through the whole three-hour meeting.
She has sat in that same chair for twenty years.
The house sits on two acres.
The bowl sat on the counter untouched.
The village has sat on that ridge since the 1700s.
Let the dough sit for an hour.
That box sat in the garage for six years.
The application has sat on his desk since March.
Three of us sit on the hiring committee.
She sat on the school board for a decade.
The court has sat every Tuesday since October.
He refuses to sit for a portrait.
She sat for Sargent twice.
That family has sat for the same photographer for years.
I sit for the neighbors on Fridays.
She sat with their twins all weekend.
He has sat for that family since he was fifteen.
Nobody wants to sit through another slideshow.
We sat through four hours of testimony.
She has sat through that movie six times.
He will sit out the rest of the season.
She sat out the last two games with a sprain.
They have sat out every vote this year.
Sit up straight.
He sat up half the night with a sick dog.
The patient has sat up on her own since Tuesday.

senses.head: Be seated; take a seat
body: Intransitive: sit never takes an object the way set does. ✗ Set down and relax is dialect, not standard American English. (сидеть; садиться)
examples: We sit in the back row.
He sat through the whole three-hour meeting.
She has sat in that same chair for twenty years.

senses.head: Be situated, be located
body: Of buildings, land, and objects at rest. No movement of any kind is implied. (находиться, располагаться)
examples: The house sits on two acres.
The bowl sat on the counter untouched.
The village has sat on that ridge since the 1700s.

senses.head: Stay unused, sit idle
body: Of something left where it is for a long stretch, usually with a note of waste — or, of dough and tea, deliberately left to rest. (лежать без дела, простаивать)
examples: Let the dough sit for an hour.
That box sat in the garage for six years.
The application has sat on his desk since March.

senses.head: Serve on a body; be in session
body: Takes on: sit on the board, sit on a jury. Of a court or a legislature it means to be in session. (заседать, быть членом (совета, суда))
examples: Three of us sit on the hiring committee.
She sat on the school board for a decade.
The court has sat every Tuesday since October.

senses.head: Pose for a portrait; take an exam
body: Sit for a painter or a photographer. The exam use — sit an exam — is British; Americans take one. (позировать; сдавать экзамен)
examples: He refuses to sit for a portrait.
She sat for Sargent twice.
That family has sat for the same photographer for years.

senses.head: Look after a child, pet, or house
body: Short for babysit, and now extended to pets and houses: sit for the neighbors, house-sit. (сидеть (с детьми), присматривать)
examples: I sit for the neighbors on Fridays.
She sat with their twins all weekend.
He has sat for that family since he was fifteen.

senses.head: sit through
body: To stay to the end of something tedious. (высидеть, вытерпеть до конца)
examples: Nobody wants to sit through another slideshow.
We sat through four hours of testimony.
She has sat through that movie six times.

senses.head: sit out
body: To take no part in something, especially a game or a vote, by choice or because of injury. (пропустить, не участвовать)
examples: He will sit out the rest of the season.
She sat out the last two games with a sprain.
They have sat out every vote this year.

senses.head: sit up
body: Two uses: to raise yourself from lying to sitting, and to stay awake late. Also figurative — that made me sit up and take notice. (сесть прямо; не ложиться спать)
examples: Sit up straight.
He sat up half the night with a sick dog.
The patient has sat up on her own since Tuesday.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Keep sit and set apart. Sit takes no object — I sit down, the vase sits on the shelf. Set takes one — I set the vase down, set/set. ✗ Set down and relax is dialect, not standard American English.
entries.verb type: action in sit down, but stative in the situated and idle senses — the house sits on two acres, that box sat in the garage for six years report position, not activity
entries.transitivity: intransitive — sit never takes a direct object the way set does: I sit down but I set the vase down; ✗ set down and relax is dialect. Objects appear only with particles and prepositions: sit through a slideshow, sit out the season, sit on the board.
entries.passive: no — the verb is intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ that chair has been sat in by her for twenty years is not idiomatic English. Even the phrasal uses resist: ✗ four hours of testimony were sat through.
entries.phrasal verbs: sit around · sit back · sit in · sit in for · sit in on · sit on · sit out · sit through · sit up

entries.meaning: To move smoothly over a surface, or to decline gradually.
examples: These drawers slide all the way out.
The truck slid halfway into the ditch.
The door has slid off its track again.
Slide the box under the bed.
He slid the envelope under the door.
She has slid the same note across my desk twice.
Ratings slide every year after the finale.
The stock slid eleven percent in June.
His grades have slid since he took the second job.
You slide headfirst only if you like broken fingers.
He slid into second ahead of the throw.
She has slid into home twice this week.
I'll let it slide this time.
They let the maintenance slide for years.
He has let his training slide since the injury.

senses.head: Move smoothly along a surface
body: Intransitive. The participle is slid, identical to the past: ✗ has slidden is not English, however much ridden and hidden seem to invite it. (скользить)
examples: These drawers slide all the way out.
The truck slid halfway into the ditch.
The door has slid off its track again.

senses.head: Push something smoothly
body: Transitive: to move an object across a surface without lifting it. (задвинуть, просунуть, подвинуть)
examples: Slide the box under the bed.
He slid the envelope under the door.
She has slid the same note across my desk twice.

senses.head: Decline gradually
body: Of prices, ratings, standards, or health — a slow slip rather than a crash. (снижаться, падать)
examples: Ratings slide every year after the finale.
The stock slid eleven percent in June.
His grades have slid since he took the second job.

senses.head: Slide into a base
body: Baseball: to drop and skid feet-first or headfirst into a base to get under the tag. (скользить в базу (бейсбол))
examples: You slide headfirst only if you like broken fingers.
He slid into second ahead of the throw.
She has slid into home twice this week.

senses.head: let something slide
body: Fixed phrase, two ways: to overlook a fault this once, or to let something deteriorate through neglect. The verb itself stays in the base form here. (спускать (с рук); запускать)
examples: I'll let it slide this time.
They let the maintenance slide for years.
He has let his training slide since the injury.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.third person: slides · -ing form: sliding (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: The participle is slid, identical to the past: ✗ has slidden is not English, however much ridden and hidden seem to invite it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all senses, including the gradual ratings slide every year
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive when something moves or declines by itself (the truck slid into the ditch, the stock slid eleven percent), transitive when you push something (he slid the envelope under the door)
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — the envelope was slid under the door, the same note has been slid across my desk twice. No passive of the intransitive the stock slid.

entries.meaning: To throw something casually, or to hang it loosely from a support.
examples: The pitcher slings it sidearm.
He slung the bag into the trunk.
She has slung more insults at him than I can count.
Sling the strap over your shoulder.
He slung his coat over the chair.
They had slung a rope across the creek.
Cooks sling hash at that diner from five in the morning.
She slung drinks at a place on Fourth Street all through college.
He has slung coffee at the same shop for six years.
Both campaigns sling mud in the last two weeks.
They slung mud until neither side looked clean.
The tabloids have slung mud at her for a decade.

senses.head: Throw, hurl casually
body: Slung is the past and the participle; ✗ slinged is not English, and neither is ✗ slang, which in living English is only the noun for informal vocabulary. (швырять, метать)
examples: The pitcher slings it sidearm.
He slung the bag into the trunk.
She has slung more insults at him than I can count.

senses.head: Hang loosely, suspend
body: Especially over a shoulder or between two points: sling a rifle, sling a hammock. The noun a sling, for an injured arm, comes from this. (перекинуть, подвесить)
examples: Sling the strap over your shoulder.
He slung his coat over the chair.
They had slung a rope across the creek.

senses.head: sling hash, sling drinks
body: Informal American, almost always in these fixed collocations: to serve food or drinks fast and without ceremony. (работать в забегаловке; разливать напитки)
examples: Cooks sling hash at that diner from five in the morning.
She slung drinks at a place on Fourth Street all through college.
He has slung coffee at the same shop for six years.

senses.head: sling mud
body: Fixed phrase out of politics: to make ugly personal accusations. The noun is mudslinging. (поливать грязью)
examples: Both campaigns sling mud in the last two weeks.
They slung mud until neither side looked clean.
The tabloids have slung mud at her for a decade.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary American: a bag slung over a shoulder, mud slung in a campaign
entries.contrast: Slung is the past and the participle; ✗ slinged is not English. Neither is ✗ slang — however neatly it would follow sing, sang, sung, slang in living English is only the noun for informal vocabulary.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: throwing casually, hanging loosely, and the fixed sling hash, sling mud
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is obligatory in every sense: sling the strap over your shoulder, sling mud; ✗ he slung alone is incomplete
entries.passive: yes — a rope had been slung across the creek, mud has been slung at her for a decade
entries.see also: cling, fling, sting, string, swing, wring, slink

entries.meaning: To move quietly and furtively, often as if ashamed.
examples: Cats slink along the fence line at dusk.
She slinks past the office whenever the boss is in.
The dog has slunk under the porch again.
Don't slink away when someone calls you out.
He slunk out before anyone could ask a question.
They had slunk off toward the parking lot.
She slinks across a room like she owns it.
The singer slunk to the microphone in a long green dress.
Models have slunk down that runway all week.

senses.head: Move furtively
body: Slunk is the standard past and participle; slinked turns up occasionally but sounds off to most American ears. (красться, пробираться украдкой)
examples: Cats slink along the fence line at dusk.
She slinks past the office whenever the boss is in.
The dog has slunk under the porch again.

senses.head: slink off, slink away
body: The commonest use of the verb: to leave quietly in embarrassment or defeat. (уйти украдкой, ретироваться)
examples: Don't slink away when someone calls you out.
He slunk out before anyone could ask a question.
They had slunk off toward the parking lot.

senses.head: Move sinuously
body: Of a person moving in a deliberately smooth, hip-swaying way — the sense behind the adjective slinky. More at home in fiction than in everyday speech. (идти плавно покачивая бёдрами)
examples: She slinks across a room like she owns it.
The singer slunk to the microphone in a long green dress.
Models have slunk down that runway all week.

entries.register: neutral — ordinary in narrative writing (slunk off), less common in speech
entries.contrast: Slunk is the standard form. Slinked turns up occasionally but sounds off to most American ears.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of manner of motion: moving furtively, slinking off, moving sinuously
entries.transitivity: intransitive — it takes a direction or a particle but never an object: slink along the fence line, slink off; ✗ he slunk the hallway
entries.passive: no — an intransitive verb has no object to promote, so there is no passive at all: ✗ the parking lot was slunk off toward

entries.meaning: To go, take, or do something quietly so that nobody notices.
examples: Kids sneak into the theater every weekend.
He snuck out the back door.
Somebody had snuck three extra chairs into the room.
Don't sneak food into the lab.
She snuck a cookie off the tray.
He has snuck a nap every afternoon this week.
Deer will let you sneak up on them if the wind is right.
The deadline snuck up on me.
Winter has snuck up on us again.
Sneak a look at the answer key if you must.
She snuck a peek at the price tag.
He has snuck a look at every present under the tree.

senses.head: Go somewhere unnoticed
body: Intransitive, usually with a direction: sneak in, sneak out, sneak past. Snuck is now the majority American past; sneaked is the older regular form and still what conservative editors prefer. (красться, пробираться)
examples: Kids sneak into the theater every weekend.
He snuck out the back door.
Somebody had snuck three extra chairs into the room.

senses.head: Take or do something secretly
body: Transitive: sneak a cookie, sneak a cigarette, sneak candy into the movie. (стащить, сделать тайком)
examples: Don't sneak food into the lab.
She snuck a cookie off the tray.
He has snuck a nap every afternoon this week.

senses.head: sneak up on
body: Of a person approaching unheard, and figuratively of a date or a season that arrives before you noticed. (подкрасться к)
examples: Deer will let you sneak up on them if the wind is right.
The deadline snuck up on me.
Winter has snuck up on us again.

senses.head: sneak a look, sneak a peek
body: Fixed object: a quick unauthorized glance. The related noun is a sneak peek, an early preview. (украдкой взглянуть, подглядеть)
examples: Sneak a look at the answer key if you must.
She snuck a peek at the price tag.
He has snuck a look at every present under the tree.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary American, and snuck is now the majority past
entries.contrast: Both forms are alive in American English. Snuck is now the majority form in speech and is common in print; sneaked is the older regular past and is still what the most conservative editors prefer. British English mostly stays with sneaked.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: going somewhere unnoticed, taking something secretly, sneaking up on someone
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive with a direction (he snuck out the back door), transitive with a thing taken or done on the sly (she snuck a cookie off the tray, sneak a peek)
entries.passive: restricted — possible but informal where there is an object: three extra chairs had been snuck into the room. The sneak up on frame is awkward in the passive (✗ I was snuck up on by the deadline), and the plain intransitive kids sneak into the theater has none.

entries.meaning: To move very fast, or to make something happen faster.
examples: Cars speed down that street all night.
The cab sped through the intersection.
The train has sped past three stations without stopping.
People speed through that school zone every morning.
He sped the whole way and still got there late.
She has been speeding on that road for years.
Warm weather speeds the whole process.
The new law sped approval of a dozen projects.
Antibiotics have sped his recovery.
Speed up — the light is about to change.
They speeded up production after the holidays.
The line has sped up since they added a register.

senses.head: Move fast
body: Intransitive, and the sense that takes sped: the ambulance sped past. (мчаться, нестись)
examples: Cars speed down that street all night.
The cab sped through the intersection.
The train has sped past three stations without stopping.

senses.head: Drive over the limit
body: The traffic offense, most often in the progressive — she was speeding — and the source of a speeding ticket. (превышать скорость)
examples: People speed through that school zone every morning.
He sped the whole way and still got there late.
She has been speeding on that road for years.

senses.head: Make something happen sooner
body: Transitive and slightly formal: speed the process, speed recovery, speed approval. (ускорять (процесс))
examples: Warm weather speeds the whole process.
The new law sped approval of a dozen projects.
Antibiotics have sped his recovery.

senses.head: speed up
body: The everyday phrasal verb. Here Americans use the regular speeded up about as readily as sped up, and both are correct. (ускорять(ся))
examples: Speed up — the light is about to change.
They speeded up production after the holidays.
The line has sped up since they added a register.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Meaning splits the forms. Sped is for moving fast: the ambulance sped past. The regular speeded is normal in speed up: they speeded up production. And the traffic offense is always speeding.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: moving fast, driving over the limit, or making something happen sooner. The traffic-offense sense lives mostly in the progressive: she was speeding.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in the movement and offense senses (the cab sped through the intersection), transitive in the causative one (antibiotics have sped his recovery, they speeded up production)
entries.passive: restricted — the causative sense passivizes stiffly but legitimately: approval of a dozen projects was sped by the new law, production was speeded up. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ that street is sped down every night.
entries.phrasal verbs: speed up

entries.meaning: To turn quickly around a center, to twist fiber into thread, or to give a story a favorable slant.
examples: The wheels spin on wet leaves.
The dryer spun for another twelve minutes.
That fan has spun nonstop since June.
Spin the wheel and see what you get.
She spun the globe and stopped it with one finger.
He has spun that record so often it skips.
My head spins when I stand up too fast.
The room spun the moment she stood.
My head had spun for an hour before I finally sat down.
They still spin their own yarn on that farm.
She spun wool all winter.
The mill has spun thread on this river since 1840.
Orb weavers spin a new web every night.
A spider spun a web across the doorframe.
Something has spun a cocoon under the eaves.
Every campaign will spin the numbers its own way.
He spun a bad quarter into a story about long-term investment.
The press office has spun this so hard that nobody knows what happened.
Rear-wheel-drive cars spin out on ice.
The truck spun out on the bridge.
Two drivers had spun out before the caution flag came.

senses.head: Turn rapidly around a center
body: Intransitive. Spun covers both the past and the participle; the old past span is dead in American English. (вращаться, крутиться)
examples: The wheels spin on wet leaves.
The dryer spun for another twelve minutes.
That fan has spun nonstop since June.

senses.head: Make something turn
body: Transitive: spin a globe, spin the wheel, spin a coin on a table. (вращать, крутить)
examples: Spin the wheel and see what you get.
She spun the globe and stopped it with one finger.
He has spun that record so often it skips.

senses.head: Feel dizzy
body: Of a head, and of a room when you are the dizzy one: my head is spinning. (кружиться (о голове))
examples: My head spins when I stand up too fast.
The room spun the moment she stood.
My head had spun for an hour before I finally sat down.

senses.head: Twist fiber into thread
body: The oldest sense — wool, flax, cotton — and the source of spinster, once simply a woman who spun. (прясть)
examples: They still spin their own yarn on that farm.
She spun wool all winter.
The mill has spun thread on this river since 1840.

senses.head: Spin a web or a cocoon
body: Of spiders and silkworms: the same word as the thread sense, applied to what an animal produces. (плести (паутину), вить (кокон))
examples: Orb weavers spin a new web every night.
A spider spun a web across the doorframe.
Something has spun a cocoon under the eaves.

senses.head: Present with a favorable slant
body: Public relations and politics — the source of spin doctor and put a spin on it. (подавать в выгодном свете, приукрашивать)
examples: Every campaign will spin the numbers its own way.
He spun a bad quarter into a story about long-term investment.
The press office has spun this so hard that nobody knows what happened.

senses.head: spin out
body: Of a vehicle losing traction and rotating, and of stretching something thin over time — spin out the discussion. (занести (машину); растянуть, затянуть)
examples: Rear-wheel-drive cars spin out on ice.
The truck spun out on the bridge.
Two drivers had spun out before the caution flag came.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: The old past span is dead in American English. Spun covers both the past and the participle.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: rotating, twisting fiber, spinning a web, spinning the numbers
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive when something turns or a head swims (the wheels spin, my head spins), transitive when you turn it or make it (spin the wheel, spin wool, spin the numbers)
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — thread has been spun on this river since 1840, a bad quarter was spun into a story about long-term investment. No passive of my head spins.
entries.phrasal verbs: spin off · spin out

entries.meaning: To force saliva or something else out of the mouth.
examples: Please don't spit on the floor.
He spat on the sidewalk and kept walking.
Somebody has spat all over this bus window.
Spit out the gum before you go in.
He spat out the seed.
She had spat the pill into a napkin.
The engine spits smoke when it's cold.
The fire spat sparks onto the deck.
That old grill has spat grease on the wall for years.
He can spit out an insult faster than anyone I know.
“Get out,” she spat.
The coach had spat the words at him in front of the whole bench.
Babies spit up constantly in the first months.
He spat up blood and they called an ambulance.
The baby has spat up twice this morning.

senses.head: Eject saliva
body: American English accepts two pasts: spit itself is commoner in speech, while spat is the older form and the one this group is built on. Do not confuse the past with the unrelated noun a spat, a petty quarrel. (плевать, плеваться)
examples: Please don't spit on the floor.
He spat on the sidewalk and kept walking.
Somebody has spat all over this bus window.

senses.head: Eject something from the mouth
body: Transitive, usually with out: seeds, pills, gum, bad coffee. (выплюнуть)
examples: Spit out the gum before you go in.
He spat out the seed.
She had spat the pill into a napkin.

senses.head: Emit in bursts
body: Of engines, fires, and fryers — anything that throws off small bits with force. Also of weather: it's spitting outside is a light, spattering rain. (разбрасывать, брызгать (искрами, дымом))
examples: The engine spits smoke when it's cold.
The fire spat sparks onto the deck.
That old grill has spat grease on the wall for years.

senses.head: Say angrily
body: Of speech delivered with contempt, mostly in narration after a quotation. (прошипеть, выпалить со злостью)
examples: He can spit out an insult faster than anyone I know.
“Get out,” she spat.
The coach had spat the words at him in front of the whole bench.

senses.head: spit up
body: Of a baby bringing milk back up, or of a person coughing something up. (срыгивать; отхаркивать)
examples: Babies spit up constantly in the first months.
He spat up blood and they called an ambulance.
The baby has spat up twice this morning.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: American English accepts two pasts. Spit itself works as past and participle — he spit on the sidewalk — and is the commoner choice in American speech; spat is the older form, standard in Britain and a little more literary here. Do not confuse the past with the unrelated noun a spat, meaning a petty quarrel.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: ejecting saliva, spitting something out, an engine spitting smoke, or a line of speech spat in anger
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in the core sense (don't spit on the floor) and in the fire spat, transitive with what leaves the mouth (he spat out the seed, she spat the words at him)
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical where there is an object but rarely used: the pill had been spat into a napkin, grease has been spat on that wall for years. No passive of the intransitive he spat on the sidewalk.

entries.meaning: To shine a narrow beam on something, or to single it out for attention.
examples: The show spotlights local musicians.
The report spotlighted three failing districts.
Every profile of her has spotlighted the same two years.
They spotlight one soloist at a time.
The lighting crew spotlit the podium.
Wardens have spotlit deer on that road to catch poachers.
A single lamp had spotlit the empty chair all evening.

senses.head: Draw attention to
body: The commoner sense in writing today, and the one where Americans reach for the regular spotlighted: the article spotlighted three schools. (привлекать внимание к, выдвигать на первый план)
examples: The show spotlights local musicians.
The report spotlighted three failing districts.
Every profile of her has spotlighted the same two years.

senses.head: Light with a spotlight
body: The literal sense, on a stage or from a vehicle, and the one where spotlit is normal: a spotlit dancer. (осветить прожектором)
examples: They spotlight one soloist at a time.
The lighting crew spotlit the podium.
Wardens have spotlit deer on that road to catch poachers.
A single lamp had spotlit the empty chair all evening.

entries.register: neutral — the verb belongs to journalism and stagecraft; the noun is the everyday word
entries.contrast: It follows light, but the two senses lean different ways. Literally, on a stage, spotlit is normal: a spotlit dancer. Figuratively, meaning to draw attention to, Americans use the regular spotlighted: the article spotlighted three schools.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, the literal lighting and the figurative singling out
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is obligatory: spotlight local musicians, spotlight the podium; ✗ the report spotlighted is incomplete
entries.passive: yes — three failing districts were spotlighted in the report, the podium was spotlit, deer have been spotlit on that road to catch poachers

entries.meaning: To be on your feet, to be positioned or situated somewhere, or to remain in force.
examples: We stand for the anthem.
She stood in line for two hours.
He has stood at that counter every morning for years.
The barn stands where the original house was.
A church stood on that corner until 1961.
The statue has stood in the square since the war.
Stand the ladder against the gutter.
He stood the bike against the fence.
Someone has stood all the chairs on the tables.
My offer stands until Friday.
The old record stood for forty years.
That ruling has stood since 1974.
I can't stand the smell of that soap.
She stood it for about a week and then quit.
He has never stood being told what to do.
He will stand trial in the spring.
She stood trial for six weeks.
Three executives have stood accused of the same scheme.
You stand to lose the deposit.
They stood to make a fortune if the zoning changed.
Investors have stood to gain from every one of these delays.
What does the second D stand for?
The flag stood for something different then.
The union has never stood for that kind of scheduling.
Bright colors stand out in that room.
One name stood out on the list.
Her application has stood out from the start.
Crews stand by whenever there's a storm warning.
He stood by her through the whole investigation.
The company has stood by its numbers.
Everybody stand up.
He stood her up twice.
That theory has never stood up to a serious test.
Somebody has to stand up for the new hires.
She stood up to her manager in front of everyone.
He has stood up for that kid since day one.

senses.head: Be on your feet; rise
body: The core intransitive sense. Watch the vowel: stood has the short /ʊ/ of good, not the long /u/ of food. (стоять; вставать)
examples: We stand for the anthem.
She stood in line for two hours.
He has stood at that counter every morning for years.

senses.head: Be situated
body: Of buildings, monuments, and trees — where something is, with no suggestion of movement. (стоять, находиться (о здании))
examples: The barn stands where the original house was.
A church stood on that corner until 1961.
The statue has stood in the square since the war.

senses.head: Place something upright
body: Transitive, usually with a particle or a phrase: stand it up, stand them against the wall. (поставить (вертикально))
examples: Stand the ladder against the gutter.
He stood the bike against the fence.
Someone has stood all the chairs on the tables.
