senses.head: Remain in force, still be true
body: Of records, offers, rulings, and invitations: the offer stands. (оставаться в силе, держаться)
examples: My offer stands until Friday.
The old record stood for forty years.
That ruling has stood since 1974.

senses.head: Tolerate, bear
body: Almost always negative or in a question: I can't stand it, how do you stand him? (терпеть, выносить)
examples: I can't stand the smell of that soap.
She stood it for about a week and then quit.
He has never stood being told what to do.

senses.head: stand trial; stand accused
body: Formal and legal, with no article: stand trial, stand accused of fraud. (предстать перед судом; быть обвиняемым)
examples: He will stand trial in the spring.
She stood trial for six weeks.
Three executives have stood accused of the same scheme.

senses.head: stand to gain, stand to lose
body: Fixed with an infinitive: to be in a position where something is likely to happen to you. (иметь шансы выиграть; рисковать потерять)
examples: You stand to lose the deposit.
They stood to make a fortune if the zoning changed.
Investors have stood to gain from every one of these delays.

senses.head: stand for
body: Two uses: what an abbreviation means — what does the D stand for? — and, in the negative, what you refuse to put up with: I won't stand for it. (означать, символизировать; мириться с)
examples: What does the second D stand for?
The flag stood for something different then.
The union has never stood for that kind of scheduling.

senses.head: stand out
body: To be conspicuous, for good or bad. (выделяться, бросаться в глаза)
examples: Bright colors stand out in that room.
One name stood out on the list.
Her application has stood out from the start.

senses.head: stand by
body: Two uses: to stay loyal to a person or a statement — I stand by what I said — and to wait ready to act. (поддерживать; быть наготове)
examples: Crews stand by whenever there's a storm warning.
He stood by her through the whole investigation.
The company has stood by its numbers.

senses.head: stand up
body: Three uses: to rise; to hold up under scrutiny — the evidence won't stand up in court; and, informally, to fail to meet someone as arranged. (встать; выдержать проверку; не прийти на встречу)
examples: Everybody stand up.
He stood her up twice.
That theory has never stood up to a serious test.

senses.head: stand up for, stand up to
body: Stand up for someone means to defend them; stand up to someone means to face them down. (заступаться за; давать отпор)
examples: Somebody has to stand up for the new hires.
She stood up to her manager in front of everyone.
He has stood up for that kid since day one.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: The vowel in stood is the short /ʊ/ of good and book, not the long /u/ of food. Learners who stretch it turn stood into something closer to stewed.
entries.verb type: action in stand up, stative in the situated and in-force senses (the barn stands where the original house was, my offer stands), and linking in stand accused, stand trial-ready, stand corrected
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in the core senses (we stand for the anthem, the record stood for forty years), transitive when you set something upright (he stood the bike against the fence) or tolerate something (I can't stand the smell)
entries.passive: restricted — fine for the physical sense: all the chairs have been stood on the tables. The tolerate sense resists like other stative verbs: ✗ the smell can't be stood; and stand trial, stand to lose, and the situated sense have no passive at all.
entries.phrasal verbs: stand around · stand aside · stand back · stand by · stand down · stand for · stand in · stand in for · stand out · stand up · stand up for · stand up to

entries.meaning: To fend something off, or, of a hull or a cask, to smash a hole in it.
examples: A snack will stave off the worst of it.
We staved off bankruptcy for another quarter.
They have staved off three takeover attempts.
One rock can stave a wooden hull.
The ice stove in the bow.
A drifting log has stove a hole in the dinghy.

senses.head: stave off
body: The only sense alive in everyday American English, and always the regular staved off — never ✗ stove off. Of hunger, bankruptcy, or a collapse: to hold it away for a while. (предотвратить, отсрочить)
examples: A snack will stave off the worst of it.
We staved off bankruptcy for another quarter.
They have staved off three takeover attempts.

senses.head: Smash a hole in
body: This is the sense that takes stove, and it is almost entirely nautical: the hull was stove in. The form looks like the kitchen appliance, which is a different word entirely. (проломить, разбить (корпус, бочку))
examples: One rock can stave a wooden hull.
The ice stove in the bow.
A drifting log has stove a hole in the dinghy.

entries.register: rare — alive chiefly in stave off; the strong stove is nautical
entries.third person: staves · -ing form: staving (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: Stove is the old past, used almost only of boats and barrels: the hull was stove in. Everywhere else Americans say staved, and the common phrasal verb stave off takes only staved: we staved off bankruptcy. The form is spelled like the kitchen appliance, which is a different word entirely.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: holding something off (stave off bankruptcy) and smashing a hole in a hull
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is obligatory in both: stave off the worst of it, stave a wooden hull
entries.passive: yes — and the nautical sense lives mostly in the passive: the hull was stove in, the bow was stove in by the ice. The phrasal sense passivizes too, always regular: three takeover attempts have been staved off.

entries.meaning: To attach or adhere, to push something pointed into something, or to become fixed in place.
examples: These labels stick to anything.
He stuck a note on the fridge.
The tape has stuck better than I expected.
Stick a pin in the map where you were born.
The nurse stuck him three times before she found a vein.
Someone has stuck a fork in every one of these potatoes.
Stick it in the drawer for now.
She stuck the receipt in her pocket.
He has stuck his bike in the hallway again.
The bottom drawer sticks in humid weather.
The window stuck halfway.
We had stuck the car in a snowbank by ten in the morning.
Don't stick me with the check.
They stuck us with the cleanup.
I have been stuck with his old laptop for two years.
Nicknames like that stick for life.
Somebody called him Tiny in third grade and it stuck.
None of the accusations have stuck.
Stick to the plan.
She stuck to the same order every time.
He has stuck to that story for thirty years.
Don't let the wire stick out.
His ears stuck out under the helmet.
She has stuck out three winters in that apartment.
Stick around — there's cake.
He stuck around until the last guest left.
Nobody has stuck around long enough to learn the system.
You have to stick up for yourself here.
She stuck up for me in the meeting.
He has stuck up for his brother his whole life.

senses.head: Adhere, attach
body: Stuck is the only past — ✗ sticked does not occur in ordinary American English. (приклеивать(ся), липнуть)
examples: These labels stick to anything.
He stuck a note on the fridge.
The tape has stuck better than I expected.

senses.head: Push a point into
body: Of needles, pins, forks, and knives: stick a fork in it, the nurse stuck me twice. (втыкать, вонзать, колоть)
examples: Stick a pin in the map where you were born.
The nurse stuck him three times before she found a vein.
Someone has stuck a fork in every one of these potatoes.

senses.head: Put, place casually
body: Informal but extremely common in speech: stick it in the drawer, stick it on my desk. (сунуть, засунуть, положить)
examples: Stick it in the drawer for now.
She stuck the receipt in her pocket.
He has stuck his bike in the hallway again.

senses.head: Become jammed; be unable to move
body: Of windows, drawers, and vehicles. The participle doubles as an adjective: a stuck drawer, stuck in traffic. (застревать, заедать)
examples: The bottom drawer sticks in humid weather.
The window stuck halfway.
We had stuck the car in a snowbank by ten in the morning.

senses.head: be stuck with
body: Idiomatic and usually passive: to be left holding something nobody wanted. Be stuck on someone, by contrast, means to be infatuated with them. (остаться с (чем-л. нежеланным))
examples: Don't stick me with the check.
They stuck us with the cleanup.
I have been stuck with his old laptop for two years.

senses.head: Take hold, persist
body: Of a nickname, a habit, or a criminal charge: the name stuck, make the charges stick. (закрепиться, прижиться)
examples: Nicknames like that stick for life.
Somebody called him Tiny in third grade and it stuck.
None of the accusations have stuck.

senses.head: stick to
body: Of a plan, a story, a diet, or a budget. (придерживаться, не отступать от)
examples: Stick to the plan.
She stuck to the same order every time.
He has stuck to that story for thirty years.

senses.head: stick out
body: To protrude, or to be conspicuous. Stick it out is a different thing: to endure something to the end. (торчать; выделяться)
examples: Don't let the wire stick out.
His ears stuck out under the helmet.
She has stuck out three winters in that apartment.

senses.head: stick around
body: Informal: to stay a while longer. (задержаться, остаться)
examples: Stick around — there's cake.
He stuck around until the last guest left.
Nobody has stuck around long enough to learn the system.

senses.head: stick up for
body: Informal, and close to stand up for. On its own, stick up can mean to rob at gunpoint — the noun is a stickup. (заступаться за)
examples: You have to stick up for yourself here.
She stuck up for me in the meeting.
He has stuck up for his brother his whole life.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Stuck is the only past — ✗ sticked does not occur in ordinary American English — and it works as an adjective as well: a stuck drawer, stuck in traffic. The noun a stick is regular: sticks.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic when you attach, push, or place something; closer to stative in the drawer sticks in humid weather and the name stuck, which describe a condition rather than an act
entries.transitivity: both — transitive when you attach or place (he stuck a note on the fridge, stick it in the drawer), intransitive when something adheres, jams, or takes hold (these labels stick to anything, none of the accusations have stuck)
entries.passive: restricted — yes in the transitive senses, and be stuck with is idiomatic and almost always passive: I have been stuck with his old laptop for two years, we were stuck with the cleanup. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ for life is stuck by nicknames like that.
entries.phrasal verbs: stick around · stick at · stick by · stick out · stick to · stick together · stick up · stick up for · stick with

entries.meaning: To prick with a sharp point or with venom, or to cause a sharp burning pain.
examples: Yellow jackets sting more than once.
A wasp stung him on the wrist.
The nettles have stung every one of us today.
Salt water stings an open cut.
The wind stung our faces all the way up.
That soap has stung my eyes every morning this week.
Remarks like that sting for years.
The criticism stung more than he admitted.
The rejection has stung her badly.
Tourist restaurants sting you on the drinks.
They stung us for an extra night we never used.
He has been stung by that dealership before.

senses.head: Prick with venom
body: Of bees, wasps, jellyfish, and nettles. Stung is the past and the participle; ✗ stinged is not English, and ✗ stang is dialect at best. (жалить, ужалить)
examples: Yellow jackets sting more than once.
A wasp stung him on the wrist.
The nettles have stung every one of us today.

senses.head: Cause a sharp burning pain
body: Of salt water, antiseptic, smoke, or cold wind — anything that produces a brief, sharp, surface pain. (жечь, щипать, саднить)
examples: Salt water stings an open cut.
The wind stung our faces all the way up.
That soap has stung my eyes every morning this week.

senses.head: Hurt emotionally
body: Of criticism, a snub, or a defeat. Often passive: he was stung by the review. (задевать, уязвлять)
examples: Remarks like that sting for years.
The criticism stung more than he admitted.
The rejection has stung her badly.

senses.head: Cheat, overcharge
body: Informal, usually passive: we got stung for two hundred dollars. The related noun is a police sting, an undercover trap. (обобрать, надуть, содрать)
examples: Tourist restaurants sting you on the drinks.
They stung us for an extra night we never used.
He has been stung by that dealership before.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Stung is the past and the participle. ✗ Stinged is not English, and ✗ stang, modelled on sing, sang, sung, is dialect at best. The noun a sting — including a police sting — is regular: two stings.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: a wasp stinging, salt water stinging a cut, criticism stinging, a dealership stinging you for money
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the person or part affected (a wasp stung him on the wrist), intransitive when the sensation is reported alone (remarks like that sting for years, salt water stings)
entries.passive: yes, and the last two senses live largely in the passive — he was stung by the review, we got stung for an extra night, he has been stung by that dealership before
entries.see also: cling, fling, sling, string, swing, wring

entries.meaning: To hit something, to stop work in protest, or to produce a sudden and forceful effect.
examples: Waves strike that seawall all winter.
The car struck a guardrail.
A branch has struck the roof twice this year.
Union members strike only as a last resort.
The teachers struck for eight days.
Machinists have struck this plant three times since 1990.
That name strikes me as familiar.
It struck us as a strange thing to say.
The whole plan has always struck me as backwards.
Lightning can strike the same place twice.
The flu struck three days before the show.
The storm had struck before anyone got the boats in.
That bell strikes every quarter hour.
The clock struck two.
Midnight has struck and nobody has left.
Strike a match so we can see.
He struck a match on the sole of his boot.
Somebody has struck every match in the box.
We can strike a deal today.
They struck a bargain over lunch.
The report has struck a careful balance.
Wildcatters still strike oil out there occasionally.
They struck gold in the second creek bed.
That studio has struck gold twice in a row.
Move to strike that answer.
The judge struck the entire paragraph.
The court has struck two of the four claims.
He can strike out the side on twelve pitches.
She struck out looking.
He has struck out on every date this app has sent him.
It's easy to strike up a conversation there.
They struck up a friendship on the flight.
The band has struck up the same tune three times tonight.

senses.head: Hit forcefully
body: Formal for everyday hitting — he hit me is ordinary speech, he struck me is a report or a legal statement — but standard of objects and vehicles. (ударить, бить)
examples: Waves strike that seawall all winter.
The car struck a guardrail.
A branch has struck the roof twice this year.

senses.head: Stop work in protest
body: Intransitive, and the source of the noun a strike and of striker. (бастовать, объявить забастовку)
examples: Union members strike only as a last resort.
The teachers struck for eight days.
Machinists have struck this plant three times since 1990.

senses.head: strike someone as
body: Fixed with as: to give a particular impression. That strikes me as odd is the everyday shape. (казаться, производить впечатление)
examples: That name strikes me as familiar.
It struck us as a strange thing to say.
The whole plan has always struck me as backwards.

senses.head: Hit suddenly, of lightning or disaster
body: Of lightning, illness, earthquakes, and bad luck, often with no object at all: disaster struck. (поразить, обрушиться, ударить)
examples: Lightning can strike the same place twice.
The flu struck three days before the show.
The storm had struck before anyone got the boats in.

senses.head: Sound the hour, of a clock
body: Of clocks and bells marking time. (бить (о часах), пробить)
examples: That bell strikes every quarter hour.
The clock struck two.
Midnight has struck and nobody has left.

senses.head: Strike a match
body: Of matches, flint, and sparks: the scraping motion that makes fire. (зажечь, чиркнуть (спичкой))
examples: Strike a match so we can see.
He struck a match on the sole of his boot.
Somebody has struck every match in the box.

senses.head: Reach an agreement or a balance
body: Fixed objects: strike a deal, strike a bargain, strike a balance, strike the right tone. (заключить (сделку); найти (баланс, тон))
examples: We can strike a deal today.
They struck a bargain over lunch.
The report has struck a careful balance.

senses.head: Discover by digging
body: Strike oil, strike gold — and figuratively, to hit on something unexpectedly valuable. (напасть на, обнаружить (нефть, золото))
examples: Wildcatters still strike oil out there occasionally.
They struck gold in the second creek bed.
That studio has struck gold twice in a row.

senses.head: Delete from the record
body: Legal, and the place where the older participle stricken survives: the remark was stricken from the record. Stricken also lives on in panic-stricken and stricken with grief. (вычеркнуть, изъять из протокола)
examples: Move to strike that answer.
The judge struck the entire paragraph.
The court has struck two of the four claims.

senses.head: strike out
body: Three uses: in baseball, to retire a batter on three strikes or to be retired that way; informally, to fail — I struck out with that job; and to cross a word out. (выбить на страйках (бейсбол); провалиться; вычеркнуть)
examples: He can strike out the side on twelve pitches.
She struck out looking.
He has struck out on every date this app has sent him.

senses.head: strike up
body: Of conversations and friendships begun on the spot, and of a band beginning to play. (завязать (разговор, дружбу); заиграть)
examples: It's easy to strike up a conversation there.
They struck up a friendship on the flight.
The band has struck up the same tune three times tonight.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.third person: strikes · -ing form: striking (the silent e drops)
entries.contrast: The ordinary participle is struck: lightning has struck twice. The older stricken survives in fixed expressions — stricken with grief, panic-stricken — and in the legal sense of deleting: the remark was stricken from the record.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: hitting, walking out, a clock sounding the hour, striking a deal. The strike someone as frame is the one near-stative use: that name strikes me as familiar.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in most senses (the car struck a guardrail, they struck a bargain, the judge struck the paragraph), intransitive in the labor sense and in disaster struck, lightning can strike twice
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — a deal was struck over lunch, the remark was stricken from the record (the older participle survives here), two of the four claims have been struck. No passive of the intransitive the teachers struck, and ✗ I am struck as by that name for the impression frame.
entries.phrasal verbs: strike back · strike down · strike off · strike on · strike out · strike up

entries.meaning: To thread things onto a line, or to stretch a line between two points.
examples: We string lights along the porch every December.
Someone strung a banner across Main Street.
They have strung cable to the back of the property.
String the beads in that order.
She strung beads all afternoon.
He has strung popcorn for the tree every year since he was six.
A shop can string that racket in an hour.
He strung the guitar with a lighter gauge.
She has strung her own rackets since college.
Don't let them string you along.
The company strung us along with vague promises.
He has strung her along for two years.
He can barely string together a sentence before coffee.
They strung together four wins in October.
She has strung together a career out of short contracts.
Two nights without sleep will leave you strung out.
He looked strung out by the third day of the trial.
She has been strung out since the deadline moved.

senses.head: Hang or stretch a line
body: Of lights, wire, banners, and clotheslines run between two supports. (протягивать, развешивать)
examples: We string lights along the porch every December.
Someone strung a banner across Main Street.
They have strung cable to the back of the property.

senses.head: Thread onto a line
body: Of beads, popcorn, and anything else put on a thread in order. (нанизывать)
examples: String the beads in that order.
She strung beads all afternoon.
He has strung popcorn for the tree every year since he was six.

senses.head: Fit with strings
body: Of guitars, tennis rackets, and bows. ✗ Stringed is not a verb form; it survives only as the adjective in stringed instruments. (натягивать струны, оснащать тетивой)
examples: A shop can string that racket in an hour.
He strung the guitar with a lighter gauge.
She has strung her own rackets since college.

senses.head: string along
body: To keep someone hoping with promises you have no intention of keeping. (водить за нос, обнадёживать)
examples: Don't let them string you along.
The company strung us along with vague promises.
He has strung her along for two years.

senses.head: string together
body: Of words, wins, or fragments put into a sequence: string together a sentence, string together three wins. (составить из кусочков, связать воедино)
examples: He can barely string together a sentence before coffee.
They strung together four wins in October.
She has strung together a career out of short contracts.

senses.head: strung out
body: Adjectival, from the participle: frayed and exhausted, or high on drugs. The related compound high-strung means nervous and easily upset. (измотанный; под наркотиками)
examples: Two nights without sleep will leave you strung out.
He looked strung out by the third day of the trial.
She has been strung out since the deadline moved.

entries.русский: нанизать; натягивать (струну, тетиву и т. п.)
entries.register: everyday — ordinary American: stringing lights, stringing someone along
entries.contrast: Strung is the past and the participle, and ✗ stringed is not a verb form. It survives only as an adjective, in stringed instruments, which is why it looks like one. The participle has also frozen into the compound high-strung, meaning nervous.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: hanging a line, threading beads, fitting strings, stringing someone along. Strung out has frozen into an adjective — he looked strung out.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is obligatory in every sense: string lights, string the beads, string that racket, string us along
entries.passive: yes — a banner was strung across Main Street, cable has been strung to the back of the property, we were strung along with vague promises
entries.see also: cling, fling, sling, sting, swing, wring, spin

entries.meaning: To move back and forth from a fixed point, or to move something through an arc.
examples: The gate swings shut on its own.
Kids swung on that tire all summer.
The sign has swung in the wind since the storm.
Swing level and follow through.
He swung at the first pitch.
She has swung that ax all morning.
Swing the truck around and back it in.
He swung into the saddle without touching the stirrup.
The door has swung open twice on its own.
Districts like that swing every election.
The vote swung against the proposal at the last minute.
Opinion has swung hard in the other direction.
I'll swing by after work.
She swung by the office before the storm hit.
He has swung by three times looking for you.
I don't think we can swing the down payment.
Somehow she swung two weeks off in August.
He has swung better deals than that with less.

senses.head: Move back and forth
body: Of anything hanging from a hinge or a rope. The past is swung; ✗ swang follows sang and rang but is not standard American English. (качаться, раскачиваться)
examples: The gate swings shut on its own.
Kids swung on that tire all summer.
The sign has swung in the wind since the storm.

senses.head: Swing at something; wield in an arc
body: Of bats, fists, axes, and golf clubs. Swing at means to try to hit. (замахнуться, размахивать)
examples: Swing level and follow through.
He swung at the first pitch.
She has swung that ax all morning.

senses.head: Turn sharply through an arc
body: Of a vehicle turning, a door opening wide, or a person mounting a horse or a bike. (развернуть(ся), вскочить, завернуть)
examples: Swing the truck around and back it in.
He swung into the saddle without touching the stirrup.
The door has swung open twice on its own.

senses.head: Shift sharply, of opinion
body: Of moods, votes, and public opinion — the source of swing state and mood swing. (резко меняться, склоняться (о мнении))
examples: Districts like that swing every election.
The vote swung against the proposal at the last minute.
Opinion has swung hard in the other direction.

senses.head: swing by
body: Informal American: to stop somewhere briefly on the way to somewhere else. (заскочить, заглянуть)
examples: I'll swing by after work.
She swung by the office before the storm hit.
He has swung by three times looking for you.

senses.head: Manage to arrange
body: Informal: to bring something difficult off, often financially — can you swing it? (провернуть, устроить, потянуть)
examples: I don't think we can swing the down payment.
Somehow she swung two weeks off in August.
He has swung better deals than that with less.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: The past is swung. ✗ Swang follows the pattern of sang and rang, but it is not standard American English.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all senses: hanging and moving, wielding in an arc, turning sharply, opinion shifting, and the informal swing the down payment
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive when something moves by itself (the gate swings shut, the vote swung against the proposal), transitive when you move it or bring it off (she has swung that ax all morning, she swung two weeks off in August)
entries.passive: restricted — natural enough with an object (the truck was swung around and backed in, better deals have been swung with less), but no passive of the intransitive senses or of swing by: ✗ the office was swung by before the storm
entries.phrasal verbs: swing at · swing by
entries.see also: cling, fling, sling, sting, string, wring, hang

entries.meaning: To walk or step, especially heavily or with care.
examples: Hikers tread that same route year after year.
Generations trod the path down to the mill.
Cattle have trod a trail to the creek.
Try not to tread on the seedlings.
Someone trod mud across the whole kitchen.
The crowd had trod the grass down to bare dirt.
He treads water for twenty minutes at a stretch.
We trod water for a month waiting on the permit.
The project has trod water since the funding vote.
Tread carefully on that top step.
She trod carefully around the subject of his brother.
Everyone has trod lightly since the layoffs.

senses.head: Walk, step
body: Somewhat literary for plain walking. American English uses both trod and trodden as the participle, with trodden commoner before a noun: a well-trodden path. The base rhymes with red, not reed. (ступать, шагать)
examples: Hikers tread that same route year after year.
Generations trod the path down to the mill.
Cattle have trod a trail to the creek.

senses.head: Step on, trample
body: Transitive or with on: to press something underfoot. Figuratively, tread on someone's toes means to encroach on their territory. (наступать на, топтать)
examples: Try not to tread on the seedlings.
Someone trod mud across the whole kitchen.
The crowd had trod the grass down to bare dirt.

senses.head: tread water
body: Literally, to stay upright and afloat without going anywhere; figuratively, to make no progress while you wait. (держаться на воде стоя; топтаться на месте)
examples: He treads water for twenty minutes at a stretch.
We trod water for a month waiting on the permit.
The project has trod water since the funding vote.

senses.head: tread carefully, tread lightly
body: Nearly a fixed phrase: to proceed with caution in a delicate situation. (действовать осторожно)
examples: Tread carefully on that top step.
She trod carefully around the subject of his brother.
Everyone has trod lightly since the layoffs.

entries.register: neutral — mostly in fixed phrases (tread water, tread carefully); the plain verb is literary
entries.contrast: The base rhymes with red, not with reed — the spelling misleads. American English uses both trod and trodden as the participle, and trodden is the commoner of the two in front of a noun: a well-trodden path.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: walking, trampling, treading water, treading carefully
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a route or a surface (hikers tread that same route, someone trod mud across the kitchen, tread water), intransitive with a preposition or an adverb (tread on the seedlings, tread carefully)
entries.passive: yes, and the passive prefers the other participle — trodden: the grass had been trodden down to bare dirt, a well-trodden path. ✗ Carefully was trod — the adverbial uses have no passive.
entries.phrasal verbs: tread on

entries.meaning: To trace and fix a fault in a system, a machine, or a process.
examples: We troubleshoot the network before calling the vendor.
She troubleshot the printer in about four minutes.
Support has troubleshot this same error twice today.
He troubleshoots for a living.
They troubleshot the whole rollout in two weeks.
Headquarters had troubleshot that office once already.

senses.head: Diagnose and fix a fault
body: Of machines, networks, and code. Troubleshot is the form the dictionaries give, but it is rare enough that many American writers rework the sentence around troubleshooting instead. (искать и устранять неисправности)
examples: We troubleshoot the network before calling the vendor.
She troubleshot the printer in about four minutes.
Support has troubleshot this same error twice today.

senses.head: Sort out problems in an organization
body: Of people and projects rather than machines: a troubleshooter is sent in when an office or a rollout is not working. (разрешать проблемы, улаживать)
examples: He troubleshoots for a living.
They troubleshot the whole rollout in two weeks.
Headquarters had troubleshot that office once already.

entries.register: neutral — a workplace and technical word; even there the past troubleshot is avoided
entries.contrast: It follows shoot, but the past is rare enough that many American writers balk at it and reach for troubleshooted or rewrite the sentence around troubleshooting. Troubleshot is the form the dictionaries give.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: tracing and fixing a fault in a machine, a network, or an organization
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with what is being fixed (she troubleshot the printer, they troubleshot the whole rollout), intransitive when the work itself is meant (he troubleshoots for a living)
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical but avoided, because the participle troubleshot already makes American writers uneasy: this same error has been troubleshot twice today is dictionary-correct, and most writers rewrite it around troubleshooting

entries.meaning: To untie something, or to release it from whatever holds it.
examples: Unbind the stack before you scan it.
He unbound her wrists.
Someone has unbound the whole bundle.
Nothing will unbind them from that contract.
The ruling unbound the state from the older settlement.
The court has unbound him from the noncompete.
You have to unbind the volume to scan it flat.
She unbound the manuscript page by page.
The bindery has unbound the whole run for rebinding.

senses.head: Untie, unfasten
body: The literal sense, of knots, bundles, and hair. It follows bind in every form. (развязывать, распускать)
examples: Unbind the stack before you scan it.
He unbound her wrists.
Someone has unbound the whole bundle.

senses.head: Free from an obligation
body: Formal, and often met as the adjective unbound: unbound by precedent, unbound by the agreement. (освобождать (от обязательства))
examples: Nothing will unbind them from that contract.
The ruling unbound the state from the older settlement.
The court has unbound him from the noncompete.

senses.head: Take a binding apart
body: Of a bound volume in bookbinding, and by extension of a technical binding — unbind a key, unbind a socket. (расшивать (книгу); снимать привязку)
examples: You have to unbind the volume to scan it flat.
She unbound the manuscript page by page.
The bindery has unbound the whole run for rebinding.

entries.register: rare — a prefixed derivative recognized but seldom produced; untie does the everyday work
entries.contrast: It follows bind. Unbound is also a common adjective — unbound pages, unbound energy — so context does the work.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: untying, freeing from an obligation, taking a binding apart. Unbound is also a common adjective — unbound pages, unbound by precedent.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is obligatory: unbind the stack, unbind them from that contract; ✗ he unbound is incomplete
entries.passive: yes — the whole bundle has been unbound, the whole run has been unbound for rebinding, he has been unbound from the noncompete

entries.meaning: To grasp the meaning of something, or to know how someone feels.
examples: I understand the terms now.
She understood the risk from the start.
Nobody has understood that clause since it was written.
He understands three languages and speaks two.
She understood enough Portuguese to follow the argument.
I have never understood a word of the dialect out there.
I understand why you're angry.
Her father never understood her at all.
We have understood each other for years.
I understand you're leaving in June.
We understood the deadline to be the fifteenth.
The board had understood the deal to be final.
Some things you just understand without being told.
Everyone understood that the offer would not be repeated.
It has always been understood that seniority decides.

senses.head: Grasp the meaning
body: A stative verb: ✗ I am understanding it is not standard, though I'm not understanding you turns up in speech. It follows stand, short /ʊ/ and all. (понимать, осознавать)
examples: I understand the terms now.
She understood the risk from the start.
Nobody has understood that clause since it was written.

senses.head: Know a language
body: Note the split with speak: you can understand a language you cannot speak. (понимать (язык))
examples: He understands three languages and speaks two.
She understood enough Portuguese to follow the argument.
I have never understood a word of the dialect out there.

senses.head: Sympathize with
body: Of a person rather than a fact: to know why someone feels or acts as they do. (входить в положение, понимать (кого-л.))
examples: I understand why you're angry.
Her father never understood her at all.
We have understood each other for years.

senses.head: Have been told, believe
body: Formal and hedged: I understand you're leaving means somebody told me so. Common in business writing and journalism. (полагать, насколько я понимаю)
examples: I understand you're leaving in June.
We understood the deadline to be the fifteenth.
The board had understood the deal to be final.

senses.head: Be implied without being said
body: Usually passive — it is understood that — and, in grammar, of a word left out but supplied by the reader: the subject is understood. (подразумеваться)
examples: Some things you just understand without being told.
Everyone understood that the offer would not be repeated.
It has always been understood that seniority decides.

entries.register: everyday — one of the commonest verbs in the language
entries.contrast: It follows stand, short /ʊ/ and all.
entries.verb type: stative — a mental-state verb, not an activity, and it normally rejects the progressive: ✗ I am understanding the terms, though I'm not understanding you turns up in speech
entries.transitivity: transitive — with a noun phrase (understand the terms, understand three languages) or a clause (I understand you're leaving in June); the object can be left out when it is recoverable: I understand
entries.passive: restricted — like other stative verbs it resists the ordinary personal passive: ✗ the terms are understood by me is not how you report your own grasp. The impersonal and grammatical uses are standard, though: it has always been understood that seniority decides, the subject is understood.

entries.meaning: To uncoil something, or, of a person, to relax.
examples: Unwind about ten feet of it.
He unwound the extension cord.
The hose has unwound across the whole yard.
I unwind with a book and no phone.
She unwound on the porch with the radio on.
He has barely unwound since the promotion.
It could take a year to unwind that position.
The bank unwound the hedge over three weeks.
Regulators have unwound two of these deals already.

senses.head: Uncoil, unroll
body: It follows wind /waɪnd/, so the base rhymes with find, never with the noun wind that blows. (разматывать, раскручивать)
examples: Unwind about ten feet of it.
He unwound the extension cord.
The hose has unwound across the whole yard.

senses.head: Relax
body: Intransitive and very common, sometimes with from: unwind from a long week. (расслабляться, отдыхать)
examples: I unwind with a book and no phone.
She unwound on the porch with the radio on.
He has barely unwound since the promotion.

senses.head: Close out or dismantle gradually
body: Business and finance: to reverse a position, a trade, or a merger in stages rather than all at once. (сворачивать, ликвидировать (позицию, сделку))
examples: It could take a year to unwind that position.
The bank unwound the hedge over three weeks.
Regulators have unwound two of these deals already.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary American, of cords and of people after work
entries.contrast: It follows wind /waɪnd/: the base rhymes with find, never with the noun wind that blows.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: uncoiling, relaxing, or dismantling a financial position in stages
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a cord or a trade (he unwound the extension cord, the bank unwound the hedge), intransitive when something uncoils itself or a person relaxes (the hose has unwound across the yard, I unwind with a book)
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the hedge was unwound over three weeks, two of these deals have been unwound by regulators. No passive of she unwound on the porch.

entries.meaning: To confirm a decision, or to keep a principle or a standard in force.
examples: Appeals courts uphold most of what they hear.
The court upheld the verdict.
The board has upheld every one of his rulings.
Officers swear to uphold the law.
She upheld the standard even when it cost her.
The school has upheld that policy for decades.
Four pillars uphold the portico.
Nothing in the file upheld his account.
That beam has upheld the whole ceiling since 1890.

senses.head: Confirm a ruling
body: Legal, and the commonest use: an appeals court upholds a verdict — the opposite of overturn. It follows hold. (оставить в силе, утвердить (решение))
examples: Appeals courts uphold most of what they hear.
The court upheld the verdict.
The board has upheld every one of his rulings.

senses.head: Maintain a principle or a standard
body: Of laws, oaths, traditions, and standards: uphold the Constitution, uphold the family name. (поддерживать, отстаивать, соблюдать)
examples: Officers swear to uphold the law.
She upheld the standard even when it cost her.
The school has upheld that policy for decades.

senses.head: Support, hold up
body: The older literal sense — columns upholding a roof — now mostly literary; also of evidence that supports a claim. (поддерживать (физически); подкреплять)
examples: Four pillars uphold the portico.
Nothing in the file upheld his account.
That beam has upheld the whole ceiling since 1890.

entries.register: formal — legal and institutional; courts uphold rulings, while people back or support
entries.contrast: It follows hold.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: confirming a ruling, maintaining a standard, or physically holding something up
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is obligatory: uphold the verdict, uphold the law; ✗ the court upheld is incomplete
entries.passive: yes, and the legal sense is commonest in the passive — the verdict was upheld, every one of his rulings has been upheld by the board

entries.meaning: To come first in a contest, or to gain something through effort.
examples: They win about half their home games.
She won the district title in April.
The team has won six in a row.
It takes years to win that kind of trust.
The firm won the contract on price alone.
She has won a grant every year she has applied.
Give him a week to win them over.
Her second answer won over the whole room.
He has won over every skeptic in that department.
It's hard to win back customers you've lost.
They won back the seat in the next election.
She has won back most of what she lost in the first hand.
Good sense usually wins out eventually.
Cost won out over quality, as it always does.
Caution has won out every time this has come up.

senses.head: Come first in a contest
body: Note the split with beat: you win a game or a title, but you beat a person or a team — ✗ we won them is not English. Won is a homophone of one: say WUN. (выиграть, победить)
examples: They win about half their home games.
She won the district title in April.
The team has won six in a row.

senses.head: Gain by effort
body: Of respect, a contract, a scholarship, or freedom — something earned rather than simply taken. (добиться, завоевать, заслужить)
examples: It takes years to win that kind of trust.
The firm won the contract on price alone.
She has won a grant every year she has applied.

senses.head: win over
body: To bring a doubter around to your side. (склонить на свою сторону, расположить к себе)
examples: Give him a week to win them over.
Her second answer won over the whole room.
He has won over every skeptic in that department.

senses.head: win back
body: Of customers, territory, money, or trust lost earlier. (вернуть, отвоевать)
examples: It's hard to win back customers you've lost.
They won back the seat in the next election.
She has won back most of what she lost in the first hand.

senses.head: win out
body: Of a side or a quality that prevails in the end: common sense won out. (в итоге взять верх)
examples: Good sense usually wins out eventually.
Cost won out over quality, as it always does.
Caution has won out every time this has come up.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Won is a homophone of one — say WUN, with the vowel of son, not WAHN. The spelling with o tempts learners toward /ɑ/.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: coming first, gaining something by effort, winning someone over, winning out
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a contest or a prize (she won the district title), intransitive without one (they win about half their home games). Watch the split with beat: you win a game but you beat a team — ✗ we won them.
entries.passive: yes — the contract was won on price alone, the seat was won back in the next election, every skeptic in that department has been won over. No passive of the intransitive they win about half.
entries.phrasal verbs: win back · win out · win over · win through

entries.meaning: To turn something around a center, or to follow a twisting course.
examples: The road winds through six miles of switchbacks.
The trail wound along the ridge for another hour.
The river has wound through this valley for ten thousand years.
Wind the cord around the post twice.
She wound the yarn into a ball.
He has wound tape around that handle three times.
You have to wind the old clock every Sunday.
He wound the watch and set it by the radio.
Nobody has wound that clock since Grandpa died.
You'll wind up paying twice.
We wound up at a diner on Route 9.
The receiver has wound up the company's affairs.
They wind down production every August.
The party wound down around one.
The program has wound down to two staff.
The huntsman winds his horn at the edge of the wood.
Roland wound his horn at Roncesvalles.
The watchman had wound the great horn before the gates closed.

senses.head: Follow a twisting course
body: Of roads, rivers, and paths. Remember the verb is /waɪnd/, rhyming with find; the noun wind, moving air, is /wɪnd/. (виться, извиваться, петлять)
examples: The road winds through six miles of switchbacks.
The trail wound along the ridge for another hour.
The river has wound through this valley for ten thousand years.

senses.head: Coil something around
body: Transitive: yarn into a ball, tape around a handle, a cable around a post. (наматывать, обматывать)
examples: Wind the cord around the post twice.
She wound the yarn into a ball.
He has wound tape around that handle three times.

senses.head: Wind a clock or a watch
body: To tighten a spring by turning a key or a crown; also of winding up a toy. Note that the past wound /waʊnd/ is spelled exactly like the unrelated noun wound /wund/, an injury. (заводить (часы, механизм))
examples: You have to wind the old clock every Sunday.
He wound the watch and set it by the radio.
Nobody has wound that clock since Grandpa died.

senses.head: wind up
body: Two uses: to end in a situation you did not plan — we wound up at a diner — and to bring something to a close: wind up the meeting, wind up a company. In British English wind someone up also means to tease them. (оказаться в итоге; закончить, свернуть)
examples: You'll wind up paying twice.
We wound up at a diner on Route 9.
The receiver has wound up the company's affairs.

senses.head: wind down
body: Of an operation shrinking gradually, or of a person easing off at the end of a day. (сворачивать, сходить на нет; расслабляться)
examples: They wind down production every August.
The party wound down around one.
The program has wound down to two staff.

senses.head: Blow a horn
body: Archaic and literary, found in hunting and heroic writing: he wound his horn. You will meet it in older texts, never in speech. (трубить (в рог))
examples: The huntsman winds his horn at the edge of the wood.
Roland wound his horn at Roncesvalles.
The watchman had wound the great horn before the gates closed.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary American: winding roads, winding a clock, winding up
entries.contrast: Two traps in one small word. The verb wind is /waɪnd/ and rhymes with find; the noun wind, moving air, is /wɪnd/ and rhymes with pinned. And the past wound /waʊnd/ is spelled exactly like the noun wound /wund/, an injury: he wound the clock and he cleaned the wound look like relatives and sound nothing alike.
entries.verb type: action in the coiling and clock senses, but stative in the road winds through six miles of switchbacks, which describes a shape rather than a motion
entries.transitivity: both — transitive when you coil or tighten something (she wound the yarn into a ball, he wound the watch), intransitive when a road or a river takes a twisting course and in wind up at a diner, the party wound down
entries.passive: restricted — yes in the transitive senses: that clock has not been wound since Grandpa died, tape has been wound around that handle three times, the company's affairs have been wound up. No passive of the stative the river has wound through this valley.
entries.phrasal verbs: wind down · wind up

entries.meaning: To keep back something you could give — money, information, or consent.
examples: You cannot withhold evidence from the defense.
The agency withheld four pages of the report.
He has withheld his consent so far.
Employers withhold taxes from every paycheck.
They withheld too little all year and she owed in April.
The company has withheld the wrong amount for two quarters.
Withhold judgment until you've read the whole thing.
She withheld comment for three days.
He had withheld his anger for as long as he could.

senses.head: Keep back information or consent
body: The general sense. Spell it with both h's — with plus hold — because ✗ withold is a frequent slip. (утаивать, не давать, скрывать)
examples: You cannot withhold evidence from the defense.
The agency withheld four pages of the report.
He has withheld his consent so far.

senses.head: Deduct from pay
body: American tax vocabulary: employers withhold income tax from every paycheck. The noun is withholding. (удерживать (налог из зарплаты))
examples: Employers withhold taxes from every paycheck.
They withheld too little all year and she owed in April.
The company has withheld the wrong amount for two quarters.

senses.head: Hold back a reaction
body: Of judgment, comment, or emotion: withhold judgment until you have the numbers. (воздерживаться, сдерживать (суждение, чувства))
examples: Withhold judgment until you've read the whole thing.
She withheld comment for three days.
He had withheld his anger for as long as he could.

entries.register: formal — legal, tax, and administrative writing
entries.contrast: It follows hold. Spell it with both h's — with plus hold — because ✗ withold is a frequent slip.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: keeping back information or consent, deducting tax, holding back a reaction
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is obligatory: withhold evidence, withhold taxes, withhold judgment; ✗ the agency withheld is incomplete unless the object is recoverable from context
entries.passive: yes — four pages of the report were withheld, taxes are withheld from every paycheck, comment was withheld for three days

entries.meaning: To hold out against force or pressure without giving way.
examples: These panels withstand winds over a hundred miles an hour.
The seawall withstood three hurricanes.
The bridge has withstood everything the river has thrown at it.
Few arguments withstand that kind of scrutiny.
The company withstood two hostile bids.
Her account has withstood every cross-examination.

senses.head: Endure physical force
body: Of materials and structures — panels, seawalls, roofs. It follows stand. (выдерживать, выносить (нагрузку))
examples: These panels withstand winds over a hundred miles an hour.
The seawall withstood three hurricanes.
The bridge has withstood everything the river has thrown at it.

senses.head: Resist pressure or opposition
body: Figurative: to hold up against scrutiny, temptation, or attack. (противостоять, устоять перед)
examples: Few arguments withstand that kind of scrutiny.
The company withstood two hostile bids.
Her account has withstood every cross-examination.

entries.register: neutral — ordinary in writing about stress and weather, less common in speech
entries.contrast: It follows stand.
entries.verb type: stative in its commonest use — these panels withstand winds over a hundred miles an hour states a property of the panels, not something they do, and the progressive is odd: ✗ the panels are withstanding a property test. It reads as an action only of a one-time event: the seawall withstood three hurricanes.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is obligatory: withstand the pressure, withstand scrutiny; ✗ the bridge has withstood is incomplete
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical but stiff and rarely written, because the verb describes the subject's capacity rather than an action done to the object: ✗ three hurricanes were withstood by the seawall and ✗ that kind of scrutiny is withstood by few arguments both read badly. Keep it active.

entries.meaning: To twist something forcefully, especially to squeeze the liquid out of it.
examples: Wring the shirt out before you hang it.
He wrung the mop over the bucket.
She has wrung out every towel in the house.
You will not wring a straight answer out of him.
The union wrung a raise out of management.
They had wrung every dollar out of the budget.
Don't just wring your hands about it.
She wrung her hands the whole time the jury was out.
Commentators have wrung their hands over this for a decade.
Farmers used to wring a chicken's neck without thinking twice.
He wrung the bird's neck and got on with dinner.
My grandmother had wrung a hundred chickens' necks before she was twenty.

senses.head: Twist to squeeze out liquid
body: Often with out: wring out a shirt. The w is silent, so wring sounds exactly like ring and wrung like rung — but ring, rang, rung is a bell, a different verb entirely. (выжимать, отжимать)
examples: Wring the shirt out before you hang it.
He wrung the mop over the bucket.
She has wrung out every towel in the house.

senses.head: Extract with difficulty
body: Figurative, usually with out of: to get something from someone only by sustained pressure. (выбить, вырвать (согласие, деньги))
examples: You will not wring a straight answer out of him.
The union wrung a raise out of management.
They had wrung every dollar out of the budget.

senses.head: wring one's hands
body: Literally a gesture of distress; figuratively, to fret in public without doing anything. The noun is hand-wringing. (заламывать руки; сокрушаться)
examples: Don't just wring your hands about it.
She wrung her hands the whole time the jury was out.
Commentators have wrung their hands over this for a decade.

senses.head: Twist violently, of a neck
body: Of killing a bird by twisting its neck, and in the threat I could wring his neck, meaning I am furious with him. (свернуть (шею))
examples: Farmers used to wring a chicken's neck without thinking twice.
He wrung the bird's neck and got on with dinner.
My grandmother had wrung a hundred chickens' necks before she was twenty.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary American, mostly in wring out and wring your hands
entries.third person: wrings · -ing form: wringing (the w stays silent)
entries.contrast: The w is silent, so wring sounds exactly like ring and wrung exactly like rung. They are different verbs: ring, rang, rung is a bell; wring, wrung, wrung is a wet towel.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: twisting out liquid, extracting something under pressure, wringing your hands, wringing a neck
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is obligatory in every sense: wring the shirt out, wring a raise out of management, wring your hands
entries.passive: yes — every towel in the house has been wrung out, a raise was wrung out of management, every dollar had been wrung out of the budget. The fixed wring one's hands stays active.
entries.see also: cling, fling, sling, sting, string, swing, ding
